Geology and Mineralogy
The North Kazakhstan gold-bearing province is the product of tectonic and magmatic events
that occurred during the accretion processes of collision in the early Caledonian period on the
eastern border of the ancient Kokshetau massif and the Seletino-Stepnyak system of island
arcs of the early Paleozoic. The Raygorodok gold deposits are a type of porphyry-epithermal
ore-magmatic system in the accretion continental margin.
The stratigraphy and mineralization of both deposits appears to be steep north dipping.
Locally, both deposits are affected by cross-cutting fault or thrust fault features that are
generally not well defined by drilling.
Mineralizationisnotwellstructured.Veinsarefine(cmscale),havevariableorientations,and
are unlikely to be through-going on the scale of the drilling. Mineralization is spatially
associated with some (not all) portions of interpreted intrusive rock types and the adjacent
country rock.
Both intrusive and host rock types can be mineralized. Structural controls on the berezitic
alteration appear to be spatial association with the intrusive rock types, their apices, and the
volcaniclastic layering.
IIIH-17

=== PAGE 2613 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
The Raygorodok deposit is classified as an orogenic gold deposit, commonly formed in
accretionary volcanogenic-sedimentary complexes. These deposits are typically associated
with island arc systems and are controlled by convergent tectonic settings. Orogenic gold
deposits are often found in deformed sequences of accreted terranes, either in pre-arc zones or
the craton margins. In this case, the deposit is localized within a volcanic-tectonic structure
and linked to small to medium-sized intrusive bodies (e.g., diorites, monzonites). The
mineralization is influenced by tectonic activities, such as faulting and shearing, which create
conduits for hydrothermal fluid flow.
Gold mineralization occurs in zones of berezitization with stockwork-style quartz veinlets and
disseminated pyrite. Multiple generations of pyrite are associated with gold, forming
fine-grained, non-persistent veinlets up to 2–3 mm thick. Sulphide assemblages include
pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, and rare sphalerite and galena. Gold typically occurs as
free-milling particles within quartz veins and fractures or encapsulated in pyrite grains.
Exploration
Quartz vein mineralization was discovered in the Raygorodok area in 1937. From 1958 to the
early 1980s, extensive exploration was carried out by various geological teams through
geophysical surveys, geochemical sampling, trenching, drilling, and underground works at
different scales. Gold mineralization potential was first outlined by the Akbeitskaya
exploration party in the early 1960s and confirmed as spatially related to
mafic-intermediate intrusives and quartz-sulphide zones by subsequent investigations.
Significant programs in the 1970s led to the discovery of the NRG mineralization area and
detailed evaluation of both SRG and NRG zones. Exploration activities included magnetic
andinducedpolarizationsurveys,trenching,drilling,lithogeochemicalandcoresampling,and
mapping. Laboratory assays and metallurgical testing were also conducted to characterize the
ores.
Drilling at the Raygorodok license area is supported by a network of fixed survey points, with
all excavations and drillholes referenced to a 1:2,000 topographic grid using local orthogonal
coordinates and Baltic elevations. Core recovery averages approximately 97%, with no
correlation between recovery and grade. Downhole surveys utilize both magnetic and
electronic inclinometer tools, with some limitations in highly magnetic rocks. Core logging
transitioned from paper to digital systems in 2015, and re-logging was conducted for SRG to
improve data consistency.
Since 2020, RC drilling has supplemented diamond drilling for exploration and grade control,
achieving around 95% recovery. At NRG, exploration involved four main drilling stages
(1996–2024), incorporating trenching, mapping, infill, and grade control drilling using a range
of rigs and drilling diameters, resulting in a cumulative total of over 1,400 drillholes. At SRG,
three main exploration stages were conducted using various drill rigs and methods, with HQ
and NQdiameter coreused depending on the lithology and RCdrilling forgrade control from
2020 onwards. All core is logged and photographed, and RC drill chips are described and
checked for quality.
Based on SRK’s site visits, review of the exploration datasets and the QA/QC program,
communication with the RGG’s technical personnel and consideration of the mineralization
characteristicsoftheNRGandSRGdeposit,SRKisofopinionthattheanalyticalprocedures
are consistent with generally accepted industry practices and the primary sample results are
therefore suitably reliable for use in Mineral Resource estimation.

Mining Assessment
RGG consists of two open pits, NRG and SRG, both of which are currently in production.
Historical records indicate that mining operations began at the site in 2008, but the annual
mining capacity did not exceed 1 Mt until 2014. In 2015, production at RGG ramped up,
surpassing 1 Mtpa and reaching a peak of 3.2 Mt in 2019. Although production declined
thereafter, it remained above 1.6 Mtpa. In 2022, annual mined tonnage increased again to
nearly 5 Mt, with 8.6 Mt and 7.7 Mt recorded for 2023 and 2024, respectively.
During the early years, RGG primarily processed oxide and transition ores via heap leaching.
In 2019, plans for a CIP plant were initiated to handle fresh ore. Construction began in 2021,
withcommissioningandtrialproductionstartingin2022.Theplantreachedfullproductionin
2023, and, due to strong operational performance, there are plans to expand its capacity to 6
Mtpa.
Mining operations employ a conventional truck-and-shovel method, operating year-round
and managed by contractors. Materials are blasted and loaded into haul trucks using
hydraulic excavators. ROM material is transported to stockpiles near the plant, where it is
blended before crushing. Waste rock is hauled to the designated waste dump.
The average mining dilution rate is estimated at 5%, with an ore loss rate of 5%. The LOM is
17 years, commencing in July 2025, with an annual processing rate of 6 Mtpa.

Mineral Processing and Metallurgy
The CIP Plant was designed by AAEngineering Group (AAE) in 2021 and commenced
operation in September 2022. The plant has a designed capacity of 5 million tonnes per year
(Mtpa), with ore primarily sourced from South Raygorodok (SRG) and North Raygorodok
(NRG) deposits. The Plant employs a conventional ‘‘gravity separation — CIP ‘‘process, with
gold dore´ as the final product.
Table ES-4 summarized the historical production data of CIP Plant from 2022 to June 2025.
Historically, the majority of the ore material feeding to the Plant has been sourced from the
SRG deposit, ranging from 70% to 90%. From 2023 to June 2025, RoM throughput has
ranged between 4.7 Mta and 6.4 Mta with recovery rates ranging between 86% and 89%,
averaging of 87.3%. The sales gold in 2022Q4, 2023, 2024 and H1 2025 was 771 kg, 4,877 kg,
5,812 kg and 3,134 kg, respectively.

The Heap Leach (HL) Plant has been in operation for several years and primarily processes
low-grade oxidized ore and mixed ore. The site is equipped with four crushing systems, with a
total capacity of 2 Mpta. The pregnant solution from the heap leaching process is collected
and transported to the carbon adsorption workshop for carbon adsorption, after which it is
sent to the CIP Plant for elution, electrowinning, and smelting to produce gold dore´. Over the
past three and a half years, the feed gold grade has ranged between 0.73 g/t and 0.94 g/t, with
recovery rates ranging from 60% to 76%, averaging of 67%.
Environmental and Social Impacts
The project’s mining, processing plant, tailings storage facility, and other major operational
facilities have all developed Environmental Impact Assessment (‘‘EIA’’) reports. According to
the provided summary of environmental permit approval status, the tailings storage facility
expansion and processing plant capacity expansion project (6 million tons per year) have
obtained the relevant environmental permits.
The project is located in a typical tussock grassland area, with numerous small forests
primarily composed of pine, birch, and poplar trees. The vegetation surrounding the mining
area is in good condition, with no significant changes or degradation observed. No rare,
endemic, or endangered plant species have been found within the mining area. Wildlife
resources in the region are scarce, with primarily small rodents and birds inhabiting the area,
and wild animals are almost absent within the industrial facility areas.
The region’s surface water system is weakly developed, and the river system near the mining
area has not yet formed. It is characterized by intermittent gullies without stable water flow
and some shallow lakes that dry up in the summer. Currently, the project’s production water
mainly comes from pit dewatering, water wells, and tailings return water, with tailings return
water and pit dewatering accounting for the majority of the water used by the CIP plant. The
project monitors cyanide levels, which could lead to groundwater contamination, on a
monthly basis. According to the provided data, cyanide levels in the groundwater have not
exceeded the maximum allowable concentration.

Economic Analysis
TheprojectionfortheCompanyshowspositiveeconomicprospect.Atadiscountrateof10%,
the NPV of the Company is USD1,400 million.
SRK conducted a single-factor sensitivity analysis. The analysis focused on metal prices,
Capex, and Opex, each tested within a ±30% range. The results showed that the project is
most sensitive to changes in metal prices.
The break-even prices (NPV=0, at 10% discount rate) are around a change of –45% of gold
price, from the base scenario prices used in the model. In other words, gold price drops to
about 45% of the forecasting prices, the Company’s NPV will become negative.

1 INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE OF REPORT
SRK Consulting China Ltd (‘‘SRK’’) was commissioned by Zijin Gold International
Company Limited (‘‘Zijin Gold International’’ or the ‘‘Company’’) to undertake an
independent assessment of all relevant technical aspects of the Raygorodok Gold Project
(the ‘‘Raygorodok Project’’ or the ‘‘Project’’) which is located in Akmola Region, the
Republic of Kazakhstan (‘‘Kazakhstan’’) and operated by Cantech S.A.R.L via two
subsidiary companies, which are RG Gold LLP and RG Processing LLP. Zijin Gold
International indirectly holds 100 per cent (‘‘%’’) shares in Cantech S.A.R.L. The
Raygorodok Project includes the two open pits and the ore processing and plant, as well

3 OPERATING LICENCES AND PERMITS

3.1 Mining Concessions
The Project is held by RGG with multiple licenses, covering the area as shown in Figure
3–1.
. Mining contract (No. 486), valid until 2040.
. 6 mineral exploration licenses (No. 663-EL, 664-EL, 665-EL, 666-EL, 667-EL and
668-E):valid until 2026.
. Geological research permits (No. 180-ГИН（ПВ）and No. 247-ГИН（ПВ）),
valid till 2026.
. License for Subsoil Space Utilization (No. 7-ИПН). Valid till 2046.
The primary legal basis for Kazakhstan’s mining sector is the 2017 Subsoil Code (Code
on Subsoil and Subsoil Use).
Mining Rights grant holders the authority to conduct commercial extraction within
designated areas, subject to payment obligations and other requirements. Licenses cover
geological surveys, mineral exploration, extraction, underground space utilization, and
artisanal mining.
Prior to 2018, subsoil use rights were granted through licenses and contracts; currently
(except for uranium), solid mineral rights are obtained via subsoil use licenses. Since RG
Gold’s mining rights were granted before the 2018 regulatory reforms, its extraction
rights are based on a Mining Contract (No. 486) rather than the current mineral license
system. However, Contract No. 486 is legally equivalent to a modern mining license.
In addition to standard exploration and extraction licenses (mining contracts), RG Gold
holds:
. 2 geological research permits
. 1 underground space utilization license
Geological Research Permit: Used for preliminary resource assessment, primarily for
scientific study. Does not involve detailed drilling or commercial extraction.
Mineral Exploration License: Permits in-depth exploration, including drilling, resource
modeling, and economic feasibility studies — essential for development but still exclude
commercial mining.
Underground Space Utilization License (License for Subsoil Space Utilization) is a
subsoil use right granted by the Kazakh government, permitting specific underground
activities. Unlike exploration or mining licenses, it covers uses such as underground
structures, abandoned mines, storage facilities and infrastructures. One of its primary
applications is underground mining, mine construction, and in-pit drilling.
Together, the Underground Space Utilization License and Mining Contract form the
legal basis for RG Gold’s claimed rights to conduct both open-pit and underground
mining operations.

4 REGIONAL DESCRIPTION
4.1 Property Location
The Raygorodok project is located approximately 70 km south-west of the city of
Shchuchinsk, as shown in Figure 4–1. The site is accessible through the international
airport at Astana 200 km to the south-east.
The nearest settlement is the village of Nikolaevka, which lies approximately 7 km to the
west of the deposit. The nearest railway stations are located at Makinsk (66 km) and
Borovoye (72 km) (Kurort-Borovoe Station).
The project lies approximately 40 km west of the intercontinental highway, A1, which
links the commercial capital Almaty with the government capital of Astana and onto the
regional centres of Makinsk, Shchuchinsk and Kokshetau and then to the Russian
border

Source:LycopodiumRaygorodokGoldProjectDFS
4.2 Accessibility
The site is accessible by road, situated approximately 40 km west of the intercontinental
highway, A1, which links the commercial capital Almaty with the government capital of
Astana and onto the regional centres of Makinsk, Shchuchinsk and Kokshetau and then
to the Russian border. Alternative access is via the international airport at Astana 200
km to the south-east.

APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
4.3 Local Resources and Infrastructure
Accommodation for the Project includes the 600-person permanent camp currently on
site.
Kazakhstan is Central Asia’s best developed nation with comparatively excellent
infrastructure including a national electricity network, railway network and highway
network which will be utilized in the Project. The Raygorodok project infrastructure is
consistent with an operation of this size and is in good working condition.
4.4 Climate
The Raygorodok project is located in an area of extreme climatic conditions, dominated
by prolonged very cold winter conditions, and warm to hot dry summers. During winter,
soils of loam and clay can freeze to a depth of between 1.8 m and 2.65 m, depending on
soil type.
Mean minimum temperature is –3 degrees Celsius, and mean maximum temperature is 7
degrees. The average annual rainfall is 335 mm, with maximum monthly average of 78
mm and minimum monthly average of 9 mm.
Seasonal wind trends show that strong prevailing winds occur from the south-west.
A large proportion of the project equipment will be located indoors within industrial
steelbuildings.Thebuildingswillbeheatedduringwinter.Insummernaturalventilation
will be utilised to cool the buildings.
4.5 Physiography
The Project is located in a very flat region, with the mine and facilities spread over an 11
km2 area. The NRG and SRG pits are 2 km apart, with the existing crushing plant and
leach pads located between the pits and CIP plant to the east of the SRG pit.
The topography of the site is gently undulating with rolling hills and ridges. The surface
generally slopes down to the southwest with the surface water natural drainage flowing
towards the Arshaly River, which is the significant watercourse in the region. Site
elevations are around 400 m above reference datum.
5 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND MINERALISATION
The content of this section is mainly sourced from the technical report Raygorodok
Mineral Resource Estimates 2018 prepared by AMC Consultants Pty Ltd (AMC), and
Pre-Feasibility study for North & South Raigorodok prepared by Wardell Armstrong
International (WAI) for the RG Gold LLP,2017.
5.1 Regional Geology
The North Kazakhstan gold-bearing province is the product of tectonic and magmatic
events that occurred during the accretion processes of collision in the early Caledonian
period on the eastern border of the ancient Kokshetau massif and the Seletino-Stepnyak
system of island arcs of the early Paleozoic.
IIIH-38

=== PAGE 2634 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
The Raygorodok gold deposits are a type of porphyry-epithermal ore-magmatic system
in the accretion continental margin (Figure 5–1 and Figure 5–2).
Figure 5–1: Raygorodok Regional Geology
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
The region is located in the border region between two large structures — the Kokchetau
median massif and the Teniz depression, which differ in geological structure and
development history. This led to a complex geological structure of the area, intense
magmatism and widespread development of faulting. In structural terms, the contract
area includes the Novodneprovskaya fault zone, which is a graben-synclinal north —
northeastern orientation.
Regionally, the area is confined within a contact zone between two major structures,
Kokchetavsky middle massif and the Teniz basin, which represent different geological
terranes. This contact setting is marked by complex structure, intense magmatism and
widespread development of faults.
IIIH-39

=== PAGE 2635 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Structurally, the license area includes Novodneprovskaya fault zone, which is a
north-northeast oriented graben-syncline fault. This zone is subdivided by the Balykts
fault into north and south areas, significantly differing from each other by their
geological structure and metallogeny.
Figure 5–2: Components of the Raygorodok Volcano-tectonic Structural Setting
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
The north area of Novodneprovskaya graben-syncline is composed of
terrigenous-sedimentary deposits of Sharyk suite, intruded by small intermediate, often
alkali-type massifs. To date, in the northern part of the graben-syncline
(Novodneprovsky ore field), one small gold deposit (Novodneprovskoye) and several
prospects (Pogashevskoye and Taskynaul) have been identified.
The South area of the Novodneprovskaya graben-synclinorium (Raigorodsky ore field)
has a completely different geological setting. The structural margins were found to
contain large lenticular mafic bodies (diabase type), while the centre area is associated
with the Raygorodok volcano-tectonic structure (VTS).
The Raygorodok deposit is interpreted to be an orogenic type deposit usually associated
with small intrusions and localized in accretionary volcanogenic-sedimentary complexes
of island arcs. Orogenic gold deposits are found mainly in the pre-arcs of the convergent
margins of the continental plate (accreted), in a wide range of crustal depths. They can
also be found in deformed sequences of precipitation in the rear zone of the craton
margins. Less common are orogenic gold deposits associated with intrusions that are
formed within the accretionary prisms of terranes along the shelf sequences on the edges
of the craton.

5.2 Property Geology
The relation of the NRG and SRG gold deposits (Figure 5–3) and association with the
Raygorodok dioritegabbro-dolerite-monzonite/monzo-diorite intrusive complex is well
understood on a broad scale based on geophysical studies of gravity and magnetic
anomalies.
Figure 5–3: Raygorodok Intrusive Complex Model Based on Gravity Data Showing Position of
the NRG and SRG Deposits Relative to Apices
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
5.2.1Structure
The stratigraphy and mineralization of both deposits appears to be steep north dipping.
Locally, both deposits are affected by cross-cutting fault or thrust fault features that are
generally not well defined by drilling.
Mineralization is not well structured. Veins are fine (cm scale), have variable
orientations, and are unlikely to be through-going on the scale of the drilling.
Mineralization is spatially associated with some (not all) portions of interpreted
intrusive rock types and the adjacent country rock.
Both intrusive and host rock types can be mineralized. Structural controls on the
berezitic alteration appear to be spatial association with the intrusive rock types, their
apices, and the volcaniclastic layering.
IIIH-41

=== PAGE 2637 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
5.2.2Volcaniclastic host lithologies
A complex package of volcaniclastic rocks are present throughout both deposits, hosting
both the intrusive rock types and mineralization. The volcaniclastic rocks (tuffites, tuffs,
lithoclastic variations (volcanic breccias, tuff-sandstones, tuff conglomerates; Figure 5–4
are prevalent. Volcanic rocks (andesites, basaltic-andesites, and basalts) are occasionally
interlayered as thin beds amongst the volcaniclastic rocks. Sedimentary rock types
(conglomerates,gritstone,sandstones) are also interlayered with the volcaniclastic rocks.
A typical feature of the volcanoclastic and volcanic units lies in their variability and
heterogeneity, as well as strong secondary alterations. There have not been any distinct
boundariesaccuratelyestablishedbetweenthevolcanicsequences.Thecomplexsequence
of volcanic environment rock types makes it equally difficult to interpret the complex
contact metamorphic variant rock types caused by ‘‘skarnification’’ and ‘‘dioritization’’
of the rocks.
Figure 5–4: Volcaniclastic Rocks — Various Tuffs
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
5.2.3Intrusives and intrusive host lithologies
The dolerite-gabbro-diorite intrusive body of SRG consists of complex mass of several
rod-shaped bodies and dykes. At SRG, thrust faulting adds additional complexity to the
overall intrusive geometry.
The gabbro-diorite-monzonite intrusive body of NRG is similarly complex, but with a
more definite mass to the west and dykes to the east. At NRG, some poorly drill-defined
steep cross-faulting is responsible for some apparent offsets in the overall intrusive
geometry.
The contours of the main SRG intrusive body are mostly uneven, sinuous, with
numerous small protrusions and apophyses. The structure and composition of the rocks
resembles the root part of the once existing large sill. The central main massif is
characterized by internal heterogeneity and the presence of xenoliths and blocks of
enclosing tuffites and tuff-conglomerates. Contacts with the host most of the intrusive
with thecontactzones(upto3m)ofplasticdeformationandflaring.Theintrusiveshave
a contact metamorphic impact on host rocks. This is seen in the melting of clastic
material in tuffites and tuff-conglomerates, which gives the clastic rocks a bizarre
patterned appearance and characteristicbleaching. Overprinting skarnification processes
associated with dioritization (granitization) are also present.

APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Dolerites are the dominant varieties of intrusive rocks. Macroscopically, these are dark,
often with a greenish hue, fine-grained cryptomerous rocks with small xenomorphic
porphyriticsecretionsofdark-colouredmineralsandaccessoryhematite.Acharacteristic
feature is an indistinct banding oriented at 40° to 45° to core axis, which is generally
characteristic of the entire massif, and is retained in gabbro, gabbro-diorite and even in
diorite.
Dolerites are the dominant differences in intrusive rocks. Macroscopically this dark is
often with a greenish tinge of unclearly fine-grained, cryptomerous latent-grained rocks
withsmallxenomorphicporphyrysecretionsofdark-colouredandaccessoryhematite.In
the field documentation are noted as diorites, andesites, psammite tuffs. A characteristic
macroscopic feature is an indistinct banding at an angle of 40° to 45° to the axis of the
core. This banding is generally characteristic of the whole massif and is retained in
gabbro,gabbro-dioriteandevenindiorites.Amongthedoleritestherearesmallintervals
of porphyry outgrowths (andesites, andesite-basalts, basalts).
Fragments of these volcanic rocks seem to define the deep parts of a large
gabbro-dolerite sill on its leading channel.
Gabbro and gabbro-dioritearealsowidelydistributed.Theseareregularly dyscrystalline
units with fine and coarse-grained gabbro texture, containing approximately 50% of
dark-coloured minerals. Porphyritic textures are far less common in the units (Figure
5–5).
Figure 5–5: Porphyritic Gabbro-diorite
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
The diorites have a problematic genesis, as most are likely to be the products of
‘‘dioritization’’ of the primary gabbro-dolerite substrate.
The diorite units mostly appear as not being fully dyscrystalline. The grains’ outlines are
not sharp, sometimes xenomorpohic. This is especially true for plagioclase which grains
have an ‘‘amoeboid’’ shape. A number of other features, such as the presence of other
rock relics, fractionally preserved dolerite textures indicates metasomatic nature of the
intrusive units’ formation (e.g. as a result of dioritization of volcanic rock).
Decrystallization of dolerites occurs resulting in the formation of a diorite-like rock,
usually of a melanocratic appearance. Dioritization of the gabbro is manifested in
clarification to leuco-gabbro or in the destruction of the gabbro structure.

Dioritization of the enclosing stratum of tuffites and tuff-conglomerates occurs locally,
starting with spotted gabbrotization or dioritization and ending with a complete
transformation of the clastic rock into a diorite-like onewith relictsoroutlinesofdebris.
Thedykeseriesisthemostrecentproductofmagmachamberactivity,whichhasinitially
formed as a gabbro-dolerite stock, and then, at its later stages, produced a front of
dioritization (granitization) along with a dyke swarm and smaller bodies composed of
dioritic porphyrite, leuco-diorite, monzonite and monzodiorite.
Leucodiorites. This unit includes shallow vein-like, and dike-like bodies, with very rare
bulges, which can be viewed as small intrusive bodies, composed of light, leucocratic,
fine-grained, with fuzzy (veiled) decrystallization of rock.
Dykes of leuco-diorites and accompanying sericite-silica metasomatites are accompanied
by zones of berezites. The dykes can be subject to berezitization and pyritization, and
therefore can also be mineralized.
Monzonites and monzodiorites form dykes and vein-like injection bodies. These have
variable thicknesses and are difficult to correlate within the succession.
5.2.4Alteration
Metamorphism and hydrothermal alteration at Raygorodok are widespread and
associated with mineralization. Injection of gabbro-dolerite bodies and extrusion of
volcanic flows had a contactmetamorphic impact on the volcanic host rock (bleaching,
hornfelsing). Along with the contact (close to a melting point), there is dynamic
metamorphism resulting in plastic deformation of clastic material, zones of
linear-banded foliation and expansion. Subsequently, greenschist facies metamorphism
overprinted the contact metamorphic features, altering both volcaniclastic host and
intrusive rock (epidotization, chloritization, amphibolitization), giving the rocks a
typical greenish colour.
The process of dioritic alteration (granitization) is considered significant. The alteration
of the various host rocks resulted in skarnification and partial dioritization. A spatial
connection between later berezitization, ore mineralization and dioritization
(skarnification) has been noted.
Mineralization and berezitization does not seem to occur without presence of some level
of dioritization. Berezitic alteration is a late overprint on all lithologies, and has some
association with leucodiorite dykes. Common in the central areas of the berezitic zones
are irregularly shaped linear-lenticular zones comprised of pyrite, sericite and quartz.
Areas of berezitization are identifiable based on colour. The base greenish shade of the
rocks disappears and is replaced by a characteristic gray colour. The berezites are
pyrite-bearing and are accompanied by a pyrite aureole. There is another type of pyrite
that is not associated with berezitization.It is interpreted to be primary syngenetic pyrite
characterized by coarse grained pyrite or ‘‘drops’’ of pyrite within the volcanic rock
types.
5.2.5Weathering and oxidation
A truncated regolith profile comprising variable Mesozoic weathered/oxidized layer of
mottledclays,saproliteandsaprockrangingfrom0mto80mthickhasdevelopedacross
the Raygorodok area. The deposits are covered at surface by barren, transported
Cenozoic sediments ranging from 1 m to 40 m thick. Transition from oxidized to fresh
material is relatively sharp (Figure 5–6). Definition of transitional material is likely to be
both subjective (with a generally low content of sulphide minerals in the fresh rock, and
as seen in various interpretations) and complex with oxidized material being depressed
along faults, fractures and porous lithologies.

5.3 Mineralization
Gold mineralization occurs in zones of berezitization with stockwork-style quartz
veinlets and disseminated pyrite. Multiple generations of pyrite are associated with gold,
forming fine-grained, non-persistent veinlets up to 2–3 mm thick. Sulphide assemblages
include pyrite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, and rare sphalerite and galena. Gold typically
occursasfree-millingparticleswithinquartzveinsandfracturesorencapsulatedinpyrite
grains.
Gold mineralization is predominantly composed of zones of berezitization with widely
developed thin quartz veinlets, fine stringers or pockets of pyrite-quartz and
disseminated pyrite. It is described in documentation as a stockwork-style of
mineralization, but veinlets are relatively fine (generally up to centimetre thickness),
low density, and very unlikely to be continuous on the scale of drilling. NRG
mineralization (Figure 5–7)seems tohave less associated veining thanSRG(Figure5–8).
Figure 5–7: Typical fresh mineralized zone, hole c-774, 137.9 m to 142.7 m down hole, at NRG
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
IIIH-45

=== PAGE 2641 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Figure 5–8: Mineralized zone in drillhole c-759 at SRG
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
The zones of berezitization are more likely to define coherent zones of mineralization.
Alternatively, a minor part of the gold mineralization is comprised of simple
disseminated pyrite and little or no berezitic alteration. This ore type is localized in
some of the sedimentary conglomerates. It is possible that this is a function of zonation
of the mineralization, as the sedimentary sequences tend to overlap with the
volcaniclastic rock types.
Sulphide minerals are commonly present throughout the ore zones, and form a relatively
lowpercentageoftheoverallrockmass.Thesulphidemineralsaremainlyrepresentedby
pyrite and lesser chalcopyrite. Rare sulphide minerals are documented as being
pyrrhotite, marcasite, molybdenite, arsenopyrite, sphalerite, galena, fahlore,
antimonite, bornite, chalcocite and covellite.
Pyrite is the most common sulphide mineral associated with gold. Several generations of
pyrite occur. The latest generation of pyrite is related to the gold mineralization and
forms short nonpersistent veinlets usually up to 2 mm to 3 mm thick, more rarely up to
approximately 1 cm. Veinlets often form a weak stockwork system with variable
orientations. Veinlets of pyrite of this generation are associated with zones of high
structural deformation and intensive beresitization. Other sulphides, if they occur, are
also associated with this phase of pyrite.
Gold in primary ores is documented as generally being free-milling. A minor component
of gold is associated with pyrite (Figure 5–9). Angular particles of gold are encountered
in quartz as well as in very small fractures and voids in pyrite. The coarsest gold grains
seem to be associated with the strongly berezitic altered ore.
IIIH-46

=== PAGE 2642 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Figure 5–9: Gold in pyrite, polished thin section, reflected light, magnification x 200
Source:RaygorodokMineralResourceEstimatesRGGoldLLP,2018
The orebody at Raygorodok is characterized by irregular zones of mineralization, often
associated with zones of berezitization and skarnification. The mineralization occurs
both as stockwork-style quartz veinlets and disseminated sulphides. The stockwork-style
veinlets are typically fine (1–3 mm thick), discontinuous, and display variable
orientations. These veinlets are often spatially associated with intrusive rock apices
and adjacent volcaniclastic sequences.
The main ore-bearing zones exhibit linear-lenticular geometry and are structurally
controlled by faults, folds, and shear zones. These zones often contain high
concentrations of pyrite, which is the primary sulphide mineral. Other sulphides,
including chalcopyrite, molybdenite, sphalerite, and arsenopyrite, occur in minor
quantities. Gold is commonly found as free-milling grains within quartz veinlets, in
fractures within pyrite, or encapsulated within sulphide minerals.
The orebody displays zoning, with high-grade gold mineralization often coinciding with
zones of intensive berezitization and pyrite-quartz stringers. Lower-grade mineralization
is typically associated with disseminated pyrite in sedimentary conglomerates and
volcaniclastic rocks. Alteration patterns such as chloritization, sericitization, and
silicification are pervasive within the ore zones, imparting a characteristic
greenish-gray color to the rocks.
The geometry of the orebody is complex, influenced by thrust and cross-cutting faults,
resulting in offset blocks of mineralized zones. The lateral continuity of mineralized
zones is limited, with some zones thinning or pinching out laterally due to structural and
lithological variations. Vertical continuity is better defined, with mineralized zones
extending to significant depths.
IIIH-47

=== PAGE 2643 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
5.4 Deposit Types
The Raygorodok deposit is classified as an orogenic gold deposit, commonly formed in
accretionary volcanogenic-sedimentary complexes. These deposits are typically
associated with island arc systems and are controlled by convergent tectonic settings.
Orogenicgolddepositsareoftenfoundindeformedsequencesofaccretedterranes,either
in pre-arc zones or the craton margins. In this case, the deposit is localized within a
volcanic-tectonic structure and linked to small to medium-sized intrusive bodies (e.g.,
diorites, monzonites). The mineralization is influenced by tectonic activities, such as
faulting and shearing, which create conduits for hydrothermal fluid flow.
Orogenic deposits typically exhibit significant vertical extent, often forming at a range of
crustal depths (5–20 km). The Raygorodok deposit also shows characteristics of
epithermaloverprintingduetohydrothermalactivities,indicatingacomplexore-forming
process. The deposit’s association with skarnification and berezitization reflects a
multi-stage development, combining early magmatic influences and late hydrothermal
alterations.
6 EXPLORATION
6.1 Exploration History
Quartz vein mineralization was discovered in the Raygorodok area in 1937.
1958: The Northern Kazakhstan geophysical expedition completed a geophysical survey
at scales of 1:200,000 and 1:50,000,
1963–1966: The Akbeitskaya exploration party of the Northern Kazakhstan exploration
expedition outlined gold mineralization potential at SRG based on a geophysical survey
and completed at a scale of 1:10,000,
1966–1967: The Shielinskaya prospecting party of Central Kazakhstan exploration
expeditioncoveredtheRaygorodokandSRGareaswithaprospectingsurveyatscalesof
1:50,000 and 1:10,000 which resulted in delineation of several mineralization zones. The
Nevskaya exploration party of the Northern Kazakhstan exploration expedition
completed an initial exploration program, combining detailed geophysical survey, soil
survey and diamond drilling. This demonstrated that the gold mineralization had a
spatial relationship with a small mafic-intermediate intrusive and was associated with
quartz-sulphide zones.
1974–1977: The Nevskaya and Aksashorskaya exploration parties of the Northern
Kazakhstan exploration expedition completed prospecting survey and drilling, The
program discovered the NRG mineralization area. These works included:
. Magnetic surveys, grid 20х10m;
. Induced polarization measurements, grid 40х10m;
. Induced polarization measurements, Phase 14 points;
. Deep lithogeochemical sampling — 45,489m;
. Trenching — 1,068m;
. Exploration shafts — 37.5m;
. Underground cross-cuts — 20m;
. Mapping drilling — 3,518.1m; and
. Structural-exploration drilling — 1,538.5m.

6.2 Trenching and Tunnelling Exploration
Trenching at North Raigorodok was undertaken in order to open, sample and trace the
orezones.Trenchingwasonlyconductedwheretheoverburdenwasthin,andwasusedin
the interpretation of the geological structure of the deposit (understanding of dyke
locations, faults, and tracing contacts).
Trenches were spaced 50m apart aligned in a north-south direction. The works were
carried out with a bucket excavator, the cross-section of the trench being rectangular,
with a width of 1.25m and an average depth of 1.65m.
Trenching at South Raigorodok was also undertaken in order to open, sample and trace
the ore zones where the thickness of overburden allowed. The majority of trenching was
carried out in the east and north of South Raigorodok. Trenches were completed across
the strike of the deposit with 20–25m spacing between trenches. Works were carried out
by bucket excavator with a width of 1.25m and a maximum depth of 4m. Channel
sampling was carried out in surface trenches from channels 5cm x 3cm in size. Sample
length varied from 0.5m to 2.5m depending on the visible variability of the section but
averaged 1.0m. Sampling was carried out manually with picks and hammers on one of

6.3 Drilling
There are two governmental triangulation stations located at the license area (-423,160
and –471,6). From the stations, a transit traverse has been completed using a Leica TC
407 to establish a network of fixed point survey stations. The fixed points are located at
NorthRaygorodok,SouthRaygorodokandTsentralnyi(Central)Raygorodokprospect.
All of the project excavations and drillholes completed at the projects have been
instrumentally referenced and controlled using a 1:2,000 scale topographic grid plan
basedonorthogonalcoordinatesandelevations(usingaBalticsystemofelevations).The
project uses what is essentially a conventional metric system of local coordinates.
Average core recovery is good at approximately 97%. There does not appear to be a
relationship between recovery and grade.
Downhole survey was carried out using a magnetic inclinometer tool МИР–30 at
intervals of 20 m. In November 2014, IES electronic inclinometers and IMMN electronic
multiple shot inclinometers were introduced. RG Gold geologists advised that some
magnetic rocks occur on site. One hole is known where it was not possible to get an
accurate downhole survey due to the presence of magnetite.
Geologists completed core logging on paper logs prior to 2015. In 2015, a digital logging
system was introduced. 100% of the drilled core has been logged. Data can be exported
from the digital system into Micromine, which generally facilitates generation of all
reports required by the GKZ. Geologists logged the following information:
. Sampling ID, FROM-TO interval and sampling length.
. Lithology, colour and texture in a text format.
. Faults.
. Oxidation.
. Core recovery.
. Drilling diameter.
A reference collection of rock types and secondary alteration is available in the core
logging area to assist geologists doing the logging. However, some inconsistencies or
subjective variations in primary logging are noted between some relatively close-spaced
drillholesinbothdeposits.RGGoldhadcommencedaprogramofre-loggingcorebythe
contractor Musyka to provide some consistency and re-interpretation of some of the
rock-types. This was partially completed for SRG and not continued for NRG. NRG
rock-types were used as originally logged by geologists.
Structurally oriented core is limited to data collected for the recent geotechnical
drillholes.
All core is photographed.

6.4 Sampling, Sample Preparation and Analyses
6.4.1Sampling
Diamond core samples
Mapping drillholes were sampled at 2 m intervals, and up to 2.5 m. Core was not split.
All material was submitted for sample and assay. The sampling and assay data for the
mapping drillholes is not included as part of the resource database.
Diamond drillholes were completely sampled in bedrock material. Surface transported
material (overburden clay) was generally not sampled. This necessitated a subdivision of
the oxide domain for the near-surface material. Routine core sample lengths were
commonly 1 m to 1.5 m while ranging from 0.1 m to 2.0 m, with a very small proportion
ranging up to 2.5 m and 3 m.
Core was sampled in accordance with any obvious geological contacts and drilling runs.
In some cases, samples were taken from adjacent runs where there was good core
recovery. Core of NQ or larger diameter was cut by diamond saw into two halves. One
half of the core was stored, and one half was sent for sample preparation. Any core with
diameter smaller than NQ was submitted for sample preparation as whole core.
RC samples
Reverse circulation (RC) sampling is mainly used for grade control and is closely related
to the distribution of gold mineralization zones. The sampling is primarily concentrated
within the mineralized zones inside the pit, with a spacing of 12.5 meters. The RC
sampling interval is 1 meter, while in some areas, 2-meter composite samples are
collected to improve sampling efficiency.RC samples were collected during drilling, the
rig is equipped with a Metzke splitter which samples 10% of the total drill chips output.
Blast hole and channel assay results have not been used in this estimate.
6.4.2Sample Preparation and Analyses
Sample Preparation
Sample preparation has been done by the same laboratories that have done the assaying
for all exploration and resource definition drilling periods.
Samples of core were dried, weighed, crushed in two stages to 5 mm and to 2 mm with
control sieving after every stage. Material under 2 mm mixed reduced to 5 kg and milled
to 1 mm. 1 mm material reduced to 0.6 kg, pulverized to 0.074 mm and submitted for
assay. From 2008, the sample preparation procedure was improved. All sample material
was crushed to 1 mm before splitting. Sample material is reduced to 1 kg and pulverized
to 0.074 mm.

RC samples were collected during drilling, the rig is equipped with a Metzke splitter
which samples 10% of the total drill chips output. RC samples were dried, weighed,

Aqua regia method (aqua regia digestion with finish by AAS) for gold was the main

using fire assay with an atomic absorption finish.
6.5 Specific Gravity Data
Bulk density measurements have been completed at both NRG and SRG deposits. The
determinations have been by Archimedean method for core samples and an in-situ test in
the open pits where rock material has been manually taken from rectangular excavation
pits with dimensions of approximately 0.5 m by 0.5 m by 0.4 m. Extracted material from
the pit was weighed and sampled for moisture content.
In the 2018 AMC report, there are a total of 544 core sample and 1,599 open pit
measurementshavebeenprovidedbyRGGoldforAMCreview,collatedfromarangeof
sources (Table 6–3), however SRK only received the measurements from core samples.

Density measurement from core is considered to be appropriate for use because the
source drillholes provide spatial references. The pit density measurements, while
indicative, are not spatially located, and currently clustered within oxide and
transitional material currently being mined.
At times, the definition of the oxidation state for the bulk density samples appears to
differ from both basic oxidation codes in the drillhole data and the subsequent
interpretations of the regolith profile provided. It is anticipated that change from
transitional material to fresh is gradational, complex, and therefore uncertain in some
locations.

6.6 Quality Assurance and Quality Control Programs
The QA/QC programme employed during North and South Raygorodok exploration
included analysis of, coarse blanks, pulp duplicates, certified reference materials and
external controls throughout the various exploration programmes. In addition to the QC
sample inserted by geological staff, the laboratory carries out its own internal QC
program.
At NRG, limited information on QAQC procedures and results are available for the
exploration period during 1997.
QAQC procedures at NRG and SRG after 2004 followed GKZ requirements. QAQC
samples for exploration drilling programs consist of field duplicates, laboratory repeats
(pulp; internal laboratory control), and pulp re-assay (external laboratory control).
CRM insertion in the routine sample sequence was introduced in 2011. The use of coarse
blanks and assay of coarse duplicates was introduced from 2016 to check sample
preparation quality.
Duplicate samples are crushed duplicates of half core vs quarter core and pulp
duplicates. Standard samples are commercially sourced certified reference materials
mostly from Geostats, with a minor part from Ore Research & Exploration and Rock
labs at a range of low-grade, mid-grade, and high Au grades. Blank samples are sourced
from locally occurring barren materials from previous assay samples similar to the
lithology hosting mineralisation. External control analysis was carried out throughout
the exploration programmes at various laboratories.
Thenumberofsamples submitted and the actualQAQC sample submission ratesfrom1996
to 2017 are shown in Table 6–4 and Table 6–5.

The details for QAQC performance as of 2017 was described in the 2018 AMC report,
summarised as below:
. Pulp re-assays insertion rate is low for the period between 1996 and 1997 at NRG.
. No pulp re-assay data is available for the period between 2013 and 2014 at SRG.
. Coarse duplicates were not included as part of the QAQC program prior to 2015.
. Sixteen different CRMs or standards have been submitted into the sample stream
since 2014.
— CRMs for Stewart Assay (ALS) assayed by fire assay with AAS finish
generally performed well.
— CRMs for Labwork Mining Laboratory assayed using aqua regia digestion
withAASfinishindicatedatendencyforaslighthighbiasofassaysrelativeto
the CRM expected values.
. Client coarse blank samples have been introduced in 2016 to monitor the sample
preparation and assay process of Stewart Assay (ALS) laboratory. Coarse blank
assay results are available for the period from June to October 2016 for SRG and
from August to July 2016 for NRG. The coarse blanks are sourced from samples of
second core halves for intervals that returned gold grades below 0.3 g/t. As a result,
the small number of outliers are deemed inconclusive due to the source of the blank
material. It cannot be assumed that the material was entirely barren of gold.
. Field duplicates were tested in 2016. A total of 297 core halves were selected from
11 drillholes completed from 2013 to 2016 at SRG.
— No field duplicates were submitted for NRG.
— The original samples were assayed by aqua regia method, while the duplicate
core halves were assayed at Stewart Assay (ALS) by fire assay.
— The results for the field duplicates indicated there is high variability between
core halves for gold.
— Theuseofdifferentlaboratoriesanddifferentassaymethodsmakestheresults
ambiguous for analysis of parameters like sample reduction and sample
preparation.
— The samples and assays, as generated, are useful as validation samples. The
data appears to be order-of-magnitude similar.

. Laboratory coarse reject duplicates were prepared and assayed in Stewart Assay
(ALS)laboratorybyfireassaywithAASfinishduringtheperiodbetweenFebruary
and July 2016.The results suggest that there is a need to review the sample
preparation procedures (and sample reduction steps) to improve precision.
. For internal control pulp re-assays, there is data covering multiple laboratories and

— For SRG, data from Labwork Mining laboratories (using aqua regia method)

. For external control (umpire) pulp re-assays, there is data covering multiple

— Stewart Assay (ALS) laboratory performed well based on the umpire
laboratory results. However, umpire results are rendered somewhat
inconclusive due to the different assay methods and protocols used between

— The Labwork Mining primary laboratory showed moderate to poor precision
based on the umpire laboratory cross-check.

laboratories, comprising 75% of the total resource data.
— Stewart Assay (ALS) laboratory performed well. Again, the umpire results are
rendered somewhat inconclusive due to the different assay methods and
protocols used between the primary and secondary laboratories.
AMC notes that the use of aqua regia digest with AAS finish for gold assays of resource
definition drill samples is not considered to be the best assay method Fire assay with
AAS finish is preferred as an industry standard. Many of the QAQC data issues noted
above tend toemanatefromtheaquaregiamethod data ortheinappropriateuseofaqua
regia method to cross-check fire assay results. The variability noted in the SRG field
duplicates may relate entirely to the different assay methods (aqua regia method primary
assay with fire assay duplicate assay); little understanding is gained about the very
short-scalevariabilitybetweenprimaryandduplicatesamplesandtheappropriatenessof
the primary sample volume.

Check (umpire) samples
Check assays consist of submitting pulps that were assayed by one laboratory to a
different laboratory and re-analyzing them by using the same analytical procedures. This
is done primarily to improve the assessment of bias in addition to the submission of
reference materials and in-house control samples submitted to the original laboratory.

to evaluate if the secondary laboratory is potentially biased. The performance of

The QA/QC program as designed and the assay results in the database are suitable for
Mineral Resource estimation.
A 30g FA/AAS method was used for the sample analysis. Some of the duplicate samples
did not perform as expected, which may be due to the nugget effect. SRK recommends
attempting sample analysis using 50g screened fire assay.

7 MINERAL RESOURCE ESTIMATES
7.1 Introduction
The Mineral Resource Statement presented herein represents Mineral Resource
estimation prepared for Raygorodok Gold (RGG) Project in accordance with the
JORC Code 2012.
SRK generated the Mineral Resource estimation domains with the drilling data using
Leapfrog EDGE software. The estimates are based on DD and RC drilling samples
informationavailableuptoDecember2024.SRKisnotawareofanymaterialchangesin
exploration data that could impact the MRE update reported herein since 31 June 2025,
SRK believes the current drilling information is sufficiently reliable to interpret with
confidence the mineralization wireframe for RGG Project and that the assay data are
sufficiently reliable to support Mineral Resource estimation dated 31 June 2025.
ThissectiondescribestheMineralResourceestimationmethodologyandsummarizesthe
key assumptions considered by SRK. In the opinion of SRK, the Mineral Resource
estimation reported herein is a reasonable representation of the global gold Mineral
Resources found in the RGG Project at the current level of sampling. The Mineral
Resources are reported in accordance with JORC Code.
TheMineralResourcesare notOre Reservesandthere isnocertaintythatalloranypart
of the Mineral Resource will be converted into Ore Reserve.
7.2 Resource Estimation Procedures
The resource evaluation methodology involved the following procedures:
. Database compilation and verification;
. Definition of Mineral Resource domains;
. Data conditioning (compositing and capping) for geostatistical analysis and
Variography;
. Block modelling and grade interpolation;
. Mineral Resource classification and validation;
. Assessmentof‘‘reasonableprospectsforeventualeconomicextraction’’(‘‘RPEEE’’)
and selection of appropriate cut-off grades; and
. Preparation of the Mineral Resource Statement.
7.3 Resource Database
The data used in the estimate consists of DD and RC samples. The RC drilling is on a
nominal 12.5 m spaced grid used for grade control and is limited to the pit extents and
was implemented for the primary mineralised material that will be processed through the
plant. The DD drilling is on a nominal 50 m by 50 m grid, with infilling to 10 m spacing
along northing. The hole location is shown in Figure 7–1 and Figure 7–2.
Data was provided as a series of CSV files containing Collar, Downhole Survey, Assay,
Lithology and Structural data. The total drill dataset consists of 1,465 holes for
156,027m of data within the NRG area and 5,024 holes for 348,935m within the SRG
Area which was summarized in Table 7–1.

7.6 Compositing
Prior to the statistical analysis, the samples were generally combined so the length of
each sample wasbasically equivalent. Thedistribution ofcore sample lengths is provided
in Figure 7–7.
The database indicates that most of the sample intervals are 1m or 2 m. A composite
length of 2 m and minimum coverage of 50% was selected for RGG. Composites were
created within the resource estimation domains beginning at the upper contacts. The
intersection thickness encountered by any given drill hole, however, is not an even
multipleofthecompositelength.iftheremaininglengthwaslessthan1m,thecomposite
was add to previous interval. The treatment of the ended composites did not affect the
overall integrity of the composited database. The compositing of samples before and
after does not affect the overall distribution of the samples (Figure 7–8).

7.7 Evaluation of Outliers
Due to the highly skewed nature of the mineralisation, the few very high-grade assays
represent a significant proportion of the metal content. As the number of such extreme
grades is small, this can lead to considerable uncertainty in the tonnage and grade of this
material. To help control this uncertainty and risk, metal top cuts were applied to the
data.
The assessment considers the variable histogram, normal probability plot, and charts
where samples are sorted from low to high and the impact of adding samples one by one
to the dataset from low to high on the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of
variation. The High-grade composites were capped or restricted to a small spatial
influence. The capping values and the impact of applying outlier capping is summarised
in Table 7–3 and Figure 7–9.

7.10 Model Validation
Model validation is a common approach for determining whether grade estimation has
performed as expected. An acceptable or preferred validation result does not necessarily
imply that themodeliscorrector derived from the right estimationapproach.It suggests
only that the model is a reasonable representation of the resource data used and of the
estimation method applied. Other issues such as the relationship between the
model-selective assumptions and mining practices are equally important when
determining the appropriateness of the resource estimate.
The following methods were adopted by SRK for the validation:
. Visual validation of block grades against drill hole grades; and
. swath plot validation approaches
Example comparing the composite data and the estimated Au grades for are presented
for NRG and SRG in Figure 7–11 and Figure 7–12.

7.11 Mineral Resource Classification
Mineral resource classification is typically a subjective concept, industry best practices
suggest that resource classification should consider both the confidence in the geological
continuity of the mineralized structures, the quality and quantity of exploration data
supporting the estimates and the geostatistical confidence in the tonnage and grade
estimates. Appropriate classification criteria should aim at integrating both concepts to
delineate regular areas at similar resource classification.
RGG has a credible interpretation of the mineralization controls that inform the
geological modelling. The lithological modelling is generally consistent with the
geological logging data and presents a reasonable interpretation of the lithologies
which hosts the mineralization.
No Measured Mineral Resources are classified at NRG and SRG project. Generally
Indicated Resources were typically in those areas of the deposit that were informed by
data nominallyon a40mto 50mdrillspacing orbetter and informed on the firstpassof
the estimate. Inferred Resources were those areas of the deposits informed on a wider
spaced nominal drill grid. Figure 7–15 shows the resource classification for NRG and
SRG respectively.
Figure 7–15: Resource Category View(Left:NRG, Right:SRG)
Indicated, Code 2 Inferred, Code 3
7.12 Mineral Resource Statement
The JORC Code 2012 defines a mineral resource as:
‘‘(A) Mineral Resource is a concentration or occurrence of solid material of economic
interest in or on the Earth’s crust in such form, grade (or quality), and quantity that there
are reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. The location, quantity, grade
(or quality), continuity and other geological characteristics of a Mineral Resource are
known,estimated,orinterpretedfromspecificgeologicalevidenceandknowledge,including
sampling. Mineral Resources are sub-divided, in order of increasing geological confidence,
into Inferred, Indicated, and Measured categories’’.
‘‘All reports of Mineral Resources must satisfy the requirements that there are reasonable
prospects for eventual economic extraction (i.e. more likely than not), regardless of the
classification of the resource.
IIIH-90

APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Portions of a deposit that do not have reasonable prospects for eventual economic
extraction must not be included in a Mineral Resource…’’

8 ORE RESERVE ESTIMATION
8.1 Introduction
The definition of Ore Reserves in accordance with the JORC Code (2012) is as follows:
An ‘Ore Reserve’ is the economically mineable part of a Measured and/or Indicated
MineralResource.Itincludesdilutingmaterialsandallowancesforlosses,which mayoccur
when the material is mined or extracted and is defined by studies at Pre-Feasibility or
Feasibility level as appropriate that include application of Modifying Factors. Such studies
demonstrate that, at the time of reporting, extraction could reasonably be justified.
The conversion from Mineral Resources to is Ore Reserves is presented in Figure 8–1.
Figure 8–1: General Relationship between Mineral Resources and Ore Reserves
Sources:JORCCode(2012)
RG Gold LLP (‘‘RG Gold’’) operates the Raygorodok Gold Mine (‘‘RGG’’), with active
mining operations at the NRG open pit and the SRG open pit. The Ore Reserves for
RGG have been estimated by SRK in compliance with the JORC Code guidelines. These
estimates are based on technical studies and operational data, with the work conducted
to a pre-feasibility study standard, ensuring a reliable assessment of the project’s
economic and technical viability.
8.2 Technical Studies
Mining related materials acquired by SRK through virtual data request and site visit.
Mining review is primarily based on the following information and results:
. The report ‘‘Raygorodok Gold Project Definitive Feasibility Study’’ submitted by
Lycopodium Minerals Pty Ltd (‘‘Lycopodium’’) and AMC Consultants Pty Ltd
(‘‘AMC’’) in January 2019 is hereinafter referred to as the ‘‘2019 FS.’’

8.3 Ore Reserves Estimates
8.3.1Resource Model
The Mineral Resource Model (‘‘MRM’’) was updated by SRK’s in-house geologist based
on the latest geological interpretation. The model was provided in Datamine format
(.dm).
Pit optimization, mine design, and mine planning were completed by RGG. The design
was reviewed and verified based on the latest MRM, which is still considered reasonable
to guide the scope of the LOMP design. The mine planning models were then updated in
Deswik software using the revised cut-off grade (‘‘COG’’).
8.3.2Modifying Factors
In accordance with the JORC Code, the Measured and Indicated Mineral Resources are
convertedtoOreReservesthroughtheapplicationofappropriatemodifyingfactors.The
primary factors considered in the Ore Reserve estimation include mining design, pit
optimization,pitdesign,mininglosses,andminingdilution.Additionalparameters,such
as processing capabilities, market conditions, and environmental, legal, and political
constraints, are also taken into account, as these may impact the quantity and
classification of the Ore Reserves.
The modifying factors applied to the Reserve estimates for RGG are listed as below:
. The Ore Reserve is based on open-pit mining methods.
. Only Measured and Indicated Mineral Resources are included in the Ore Reserve
estimate.
. The scope of the Ore Reserves estimation considers the boundaries of the mining
license and near-by existing infrastructure.
. Pit optimization takes into account various factors, such as overall slope angle,
mining costs, processing costs, recovery rates, and metal prices.
. The selection of the optimal pit shell is based on RGG’s strategic decision.
. The detailed pit design is guided by the selected optimal pit shell and considering
the different design parameters.

9 MINING METHODS
9.1 Introduction
RGG comprises two open pits: NRG and SRG. Both pits are currently in production.
According to the final feasibility study completed by Lycopodium in 2019, the designed
processing capacity is at least 5 Mtpa.
Historical production records show that mining activities commenced at the site in 2008;
however,annualmining capacity did notexceed1 Mt until 2014.In 2015,mining ratesat
RGG began to ramp up, surpassing 1 Mtpa and peaking at 3.2 Mt in 2019. Production
subsequently declined but remained above 1.6 Mtpa. In 2022, annual mined tonnage
increased again, reaching nearly 5 Mt, while 2023 and 2024 annual production was
reported at 8.6 Mt and 7.7 Mt, respectively.
In the early stages, RGG primarily processed oxide and transition ores using heap
leaching. In 2019, planning for a CIP (‘‘Carbon-in-Pulp’’) plant commenced in order to
treat fresh ore, with a design capacity of 5 Mtpa. Construction of the CIP plant began in
2021, with commissioning and trial production starting in 2022. The plant reached full
production in 2023, and, given the strong production performance, plans are in place to
increase the CIP plant capacity to 6 Mtpa.
As of 30 June 2024, a total of 14 Mt of oxide ore averaging 0.93 g/t Au (containing
approximately 13 tonnes of gold), 7 Mt of transition ore averaging 0.91 g/t Au
(containing approximately 6 tonnes of gold), and 18 Mt of fresh ore averaging 1.06 g/t
Au (containing 19 tonnes of gold) have been mined from the NRG and SRG pits
combined. In total, RGG has produced 39 Mt of ore at an average grade of 0.99 g/t Au,
with a contained gold content of 38 tonnes.
Historical mining production data for RGG from 2008 to 2024 is presented in Figure
9–1, Figure 9–2 and Figure 9–3.

9.2 Hydrogeology
RGG project is situated in an area characterized by extreme climatic conditions, with
long and very cold winters, and warm to hot, dry summers. In winter, the surface soils at
the project site — composed mainly of loam and clay — can freeze to depths ranging
from 1.8 to 2.65 meters, depending on soil type.
According to the 2024 Reserve Report, the site’s hydrogeological conditions are
complex. Deformation, faults, and fractures are common. Both the bedrock and
heavily weathered rocks typically exhibit very low permeability. The main aquifers are
associated with fractured zones and faults, which govern groundwater storage and
transport. Faults may also enhance the depth of weathering into the bedrock. Due to the
high degree of weathering of surface rocks, recharge from precipitation is limited.
IIIH-102

=== PAGE 2698 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
In 2024, ITASCA reviewed the historical hydrogeological work at RGG and developed a
numerical model as part of the slope stability analyses. The findings from 2024
Hydrogeology are summarized below:
. Groundwater Flow Direction: Groundwater generally flows westward toward the
Arshaly River, which acts as the regional discharge area.
. Cone of Depression Effects: Mining activities have created two cones of depression
around NRG and SRG, impacting local groundwater flow.
. Definition of Hydrogeological Units: It is recommended that hydrogeological units
be defined based on geotechnical engineering units, with further hydrogeological
subdivisions applied as required for improved slope stability analysis.
. Permeability Variations: The highest permeability is found in weathered rock
layers, while clay layers have the lowest permeability. These contrasts significantly
affect the accuracy of the hydrogeological model.
. Monitoring and Testing Improvements: It is recommended that packer testing be
performed during drilling, and that Vibrating Wire piezometers be installed within
the pits to monitor pore water pressures within the rock mass.
. Model Updates and Calibration: The hydrogeological model should be regularly
updated and calibrated to incorporate the latest data and research findings,
ensuring continued model accuracy and reliability.
9.2.1Dewatering
Accordingtothe2024ReserveReport,groundwateristypically foundatshallowdepths,
ranging from 1.2 to 15.3 meters, with an average depth of 4.9 meters. The project
employs a combination of in-pit and external dewatering systems. The planned
dewatering strategy involves the installation of dewatering boreholes around the
perimeter of each pit, with five boreholes anticipated per pit. Each borehole will have
a maximum depth of 164 meters and a dewatering capacity of 54 m3 per hour.
According to RGG, between July 2023 and June 2025, the average monthly dewatering
volumeswere99,000m3forNRGand157,000m3forSRG.Thepeakdewateringoutflow
occurred in April 2024, with NRG reaching 153,000 m3 and SRG 238,000 m3. The
monthly water outflow at RGG is shown in Figure 9–4. Monitoring equipment has been
installed on the eastern side of NRG to continuously monitor areas not scheduled for
mining.
It is recommended that the dewatering system be designed with sufficient redundancy.
Pump stationsshould be sized to handle peak flows, and onsite drainage channels should
beequippedforfloodcontroltoensuresafewaterdischargeevenduringextremeweather
events.

Optimization Inputs Parameters
AMC utilized the Whittle software for open pit optimization with Lerchs-Grossman
algorithm. In general terms, Whittle adjusts the base input price by a range of revenue
factors(‘‘RF’’),bothaboveandbelowabasevalueof1.ForeachRF,Whittlegeneratesa
three-dimensionalshapepitshell,thatmaximizesthevaluebasedonallinputparameters
andtheadjusted price.Lower RFproducesmaller shells, whilehigherRF resultin larger
shells. This approach creates a series of ’nested’ shells, with each shell contained within
the next larger one. A summary of the pit optimization parameters for RGG are
presented in Table 8–1. Except for the gold price, for which AMC used USD1,750/oz.
Optimization Results
A series of nested pit shells were generated based on a range of RF on gold price.
Eventually, AMC selected RF at 0.86 pit shell as the basis of the NRG open pit design
and RF at 0.88 pit shell was also selected as the basis of the SRG open pit design.
NRG Results
SRK re-ran the pit optimization to verify the reasonableness of the previous LOMP. It is
important to note the following constraints:
. The gold price of USD2,200/oz was used during the pit optimization re-run.
. On the north-west side of NRG, there is a historical waste rock dump (‘‘WRD’’)
with an approximate height of 40 metres. A safety factor of 1.5 was applied,
resulting in a buffer zone of 60 metres (implemented as a heavy block constraint) to
prevent re-excavation of this waste.
. On the south-east side of NRG, there is an operational WRD with a design height
of approximately 80 metres. A safety factor of 1.5 was applied, resulting in a buffer
zone of 120 metres (implemented as a heavy block constraint) to avoid the need to
relocate this WRD.

considered reasonable for guiding ore reserve estimation.
Pit Stage Selection
Pit staging limits were designed to maximize undiscounted operating cash flow by
deferring waste stripping and material movement while ensuring consistent plant feed,
targeting approximately two years of feed (10–20 Mt). A total of four pit stages were
designed for both SRG and NRG, each with a target minimum mining width of 50
metres.

9.4.3Material Logistics
Both the NRG and SRG deposits are planned as open-pit mines. An excavator-truck
fleet is employed for the transportation of both ore and waste to their designated
destinations, a system commonly adopted in open-pit operations. SRK considers this
approach to be generally appropriate for the overall mine development.
Within the pits, ore and waste are hauled using conventional truck-and-roadway
methods. The maximum road gradient is limited to 10%, and ramp exits are strategically
located near waste dumps and ROM stockpiles to minimize travel distances. The haul
distance from the pit exit to the ROM stockpile is approximately 2.5 km for NRG and
about 0.7 km for SRG. For NRG, 34.7-tonne haul trucks are primarily used, while SRG
utilizes larger 91.7-tonne trucks.
As mining progresses, haul distances are expected to gradually increase due to deepening
of the pit and the sequential development of the final pit limits.

9.5 Mine Production Plan
Sincethecut-offgradehasbeenupdated,themineproductionplanhasalsobeenrevised.
The updated schedule was developed using the Deswik software suite, which aggregates
pit inventory by stage, bench, and designated material bins. To ensure the required level
of detail and prioritization, several grade bins have been assigned for ROM materials in
line with the company’s current blending strategy, as outlined below:
. Super High Grade (SHG): >1.5 g/t Au
. High Grade (HG): 1.1–1.5 g/t Au
. Medium Grade (MG): 0.8–1.1 g/t Au
. Low Grade (LG): 0.5–0.8 g/t Au
. Lean Grade (LO): COG to 0.5 g/t Au
Itisimportanttonotethatmaterialassignedtotheleangradeorebindoesnotfallbelow
the COG.
The mining and blending schedule are organized on a monthly basis and reported
annually. The following assumptions were applied during production scheduling:
. Only blocks classified as Measured and Indicated Mineral Resources with a gold
grade above the COG are considered and treated as ROM material.
. Blocks classified as Inferred Mineral Resources, those with a gold grade below the
COG, and sterilized materials are treated as waste.
. Oxide and transition materials are not treated separately, as all material will be
processed together; only grade differences are considered in processing.
. FourcutbacksareplannedforbothNRGandSRGtoensureastableROMsupply.
. The maximum annual total material movement (‘‘TMM’’) is based on the current
fleet size and its performance.
. The vertical lag between mining phases is restricted to a maximum of 80 meters.

9.6 Conclusion and Recommendations
RGG is planned as an open-pit operation. SRK conducted pit optimization to review the
current LOMP design, verified its reasonableness, and updated the LOM plan to guide
the extraction of eligible Mineral Resources. The open-pit mining method employed at
bothNRGandSRGfollowstheconventionalapproachofdrillingandblasting,followed
by loading and hauling. After reviewing the methodology, equipment list, and mining
services, SRK considers the mine to be operating in line with industry’s best practices.
RGG will primarily rely on contractors for both stripping and mining activities. The
mine will provide management, technical services, and supervisory staff to oversee
operations. The primary production mobile equipment, along with some ancillary
equipment, will be supplied by the mining contractor.
Overall, the mining methods applied at RGG are considered sufficient and reasonable to
support ongoing and future operations. Below are the recommendations:
. Preliminaryreviewindicatesthatnearbyinfrastructuredoesnotposealimitationto
the expansion of NRG. However, it is recommended to carry out further geological
investigations in the northern part of the pit to better define the lithology, as this
will affect the design of the ultimate pit boundary.
. ForSRG,preliminaryassessmentsuggeststhatnearbyinfrastructureisasignificant
constraint to expansion of the pit boundary. It is recommended that additional
trade-off studies are conducted before proceeding with any new pit design.
10 MINERAL PROCESSING AND METALLURGY
10.1 Overview
The RGG Carbon-in-Pulp (CIP) Plant was designed by AAEngineering Group (AAE) in
2021 and commenced operation in September 2022. The plant has a designed capacity of
5 million tonnes per year (Mtpa), with ore primarily sourced from South Raygorodok
(SRG) and North Raygorodok (NRG) deposits. The plant employs a conventional
‘‘gravity separation — CIP’’ process, with gold dore´ as the final product. From 2023 to
June2025,RoMthroughputhasrangedbetween4.7Mtaand6.4Mtawithrecoveryrates
ranging between 86% and 89%, averaging of 87.3%. The sales gold in 2022 Q4, 2023,
2024 and H1 2025 was 771 kg, 4,877 kg, 5,812 kg and 3,134 kg, respectively.
The Heap Leach (HL) Plant has been in operation for several years and primarily
processes low-grade oxidized ore and mixed ore. The site is equipped with four crushing
systems, with a total capacity of 2 Mpta. The pregnant solution from the heap leaching
process is collected and transported to the carbon adsorption workshop for carbon
adsorption, after which it is sent to the CIP Plant for elution, electrowinning, and
smelting to produce gold dore´. Over the past three and a half years, the feed gold grade
has ranged between 0.73 g/t and 0.94 g/t, with recovery rates ranging from 60% to 76%,
averaging of 67%.

10.2.1Introduction
In 2018, SGS was commissioned to carry out four stages of metallurgical tests on
variability samples from SRG and NRG, which served as the basis for the design. The
main programs were as follows:
. Study the physical and mechanical properties of the samples (Stage 1);
. Investigate the metallurgical properties of variability composite samples (Stage 2);
and

The mineralogy research results yield the following conclusions:
. The average gold and silver grades of the SRG sample are 1.18 g/t and 0.60 g/t,
respectively, while the average gold and silver grades of the NRG sample are 0.98
g/t and 0.75 g/t, respectively.
. The sulfur content in the samples is 2.20% and 0.31%, respectively, and the
oxidation rates are 7.2% and 20.5%, respectively. The ore type is low-grade sulfide
gold-bearing ore, with the SRG sample having a lower oxidation rate compared to
the NRG sample.
. The organic carbon content in the SRG sample (0.08%) is slightly higher than that
in the NRG sample. (0.05%).
. The main metallic minerals in the samples are pyrite (approximately 3%),
magnetite, and hematite (approximately 4%). Chalcopyrite, sphalerite, and
galena are present in lower amounts, with their average cumulative contents not
exceeding 0.041% and 0.16%, respectively. The main non-metallic minerals are
quartz, tremolite, albite, orthoclase, chlorite, dolomite, calcite, and muscovite.
. Gold and silver are the primary recoverable valuable elements, mainly associated
with pyrite, galena, and quartz.

10.2.3Comminution Test
The purpose of this test is to provide technical parameters for the design of the grinding

results summarized in Table 10–2. The value Axb is a measure of resistance to impact
breakage, and low values are indicative of hard ores, while high values indicate soft ores.

are classified as ‘‘hard to very hard’’ ore types, indicating that the ore is relatively
difficult to grind. Overall, the SRG ore samples are harder and more difficult to grind
compared to the NRG ore samples.
