10.3 Processing Practice
10.3.1Process Flowsheet
The CIP Plant production flowsheet consists of two-stage crushing, high pressure
grinding (HPGR), one-stage grinding, gravity recovery by Knelson & Acacia, CIP of
gravity tailings, and gold loaded carbon elution & electrowinning & smelting. The
process technology is traditional and mature, which is considered to be relatively
reasonable for treating the ore from RG mine.
The simplified flowsheet is demonstrated in Figure 10–1, and specified as follows:
Crushing and Screening
The run-of-mine (ROM) ore is transported from the SRG and NRG open pits or ore
stockpiles to the ROM bin or ROM stockpile. A two-stage closed-circuit crushing and
screening process is employed. The maximum particle size of the ROM ore is 900 mm
(F = 900 mm), and the crushed product size is less than 40 mm (P = 31 mm). A
100 80
crushed product stockpile with a capacity of 7,788 tonnes is set up between the crushing
system and the HPGR system to serve as a buffer.
IIIH-124

=== PAGE 2720 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
HPGR
The crushed ore is fed into the HPGR for further comminution and then sent to a
double-deck screen for screening (screen aperture sizes: 40 mm/8 mm). According to the
originaldesign,materiallargerthan40mmwastobesenttoatertiarycrusher.However,
production practices revealed that there was almost no material on the top deck, and the
tertiary crusher has since been decommissioned. As a result, the oversize material from
both screen decks is returned to the HPGR. The final product from the HPGR has a
particle size of less than 8 mm (P = 5.2 mm) and is conveyed to the fine ore buffer bin
80
before grinding.
Grinding and Classification
The grinding and classification process is carried out in two series, using a single-stage
closed-circuit grinding system. The grinding pulp density is approximately 70%, and the
product grinding fineness is P = 80 μm. Lime is directly added to the mill to adjust the
80
slurry pH. The underflow from the hydrocyclone is returned to the mill, while the
overflow is sent to a trash screen prior to pre-leach thickening.
Gravity Recovery
Based on the head grade of gold and actual production conditions, a bypass system is set
up for the grinding product to feed into the gravity concentration system, allowing for
theearlyrecoveryofcoarse-grainedgold.Acoarseparticlescreen(witha2mmaperture)
is installed before the Knelson concentrator. The oversize material from the screen is
returned to the mill, while the undersize material is fed into the gravity concentration
system. The tailings from the gravity concentration process are returned to the mill, and
the gravity gold concentrate is sent to the Acacia system for intensive leaching and
electrowinning, producing gold sludge. The gold sludge is then processed in the smelting
system to produce gold dore´.
Pre-Leach Thickening
Trash is removed from the cyclone overflow ahead of the pre — leach thickener by a
vibrating screen (aperture size: 0.8 mm). The trash is discharged into a bin for disposal.
The screen underflow gravitates to the pre — leach thickener feed. The thickener
underflow (pulp concentration of about 50%) is pumped to the pre-leaching tank of the
CIP circuit. The thickener overflow gravity flows to the process water tank.
Leaching and Adsorption Circuit
The slurry is dewatered in a thickener before being fed into four leach tanks (each with a
capacity of 5,050 m3) for leaching, with a leaching time of approximately 20 hours and a
pH value greater than 10. After leaching, the slurry flows into seven adsorption tanks
(each with a capacity of 200 m3), where activated carbon is added for gold adsorption.
The adsorption time is about 24 hours, and the activated carbon concentration is
approximately40 g/L.Onceadsorptionis complete,the gold-loaded carbon is sentto the
acid washing, elution, and electrowinning system. The slurry is passed through a safety
screen (with a 0.6 mm aperture) to recover fine carbon before being transported to the
tailings system.
IIIH-125

=== PAGE 2721 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Elution and Carbon Regeneration
Thegold—loadedcarbonenterstotheacidtreatmentvesselandiswashedwith3%HCl
to remove inorganic impurities and then transferred to the elution column. The
Anglo-American Research Laboratory method (AARL) elution process is employed and
sodium cyanide and NaOH aqueous solution (2% NaOH + 3% NaCN) are used as
elution liquid, with the elution time for about 11 hours. The pregnant solution from the
elution circuit will be collected in an elution pregnant solution tank.
After desorption, the carbon is re-generated in a carbon regeneration kiln system (700 —
800℃) to drive off the organic and inorganic contaminants and then returned to the CIP
circuit for reuse.
Electrowinning and Smelting
The gold pregnant solution is passed through three electrowinning cells equipped with
stainless steel cathodes. The loaded cathodes are pressure washed, and the gold sludge is
filtered and dried, and then smelted onsite to produce gold dore´.
Tailings Cyanide Destruction
TheCIPtailingsslurrywillflowtotwocyanidedestructiontanks.Thefreecyanideinthe
tailings is decomposed by the INCO method, with the reagents of Sodium Metabisulfite
(SMBS), copper sulphate and lime slurry. The tailings Weak Acid Dissociable (WAD)
cyanide content is less than 50 ppm after cyanide destruction, which meets the minimum
standards of ICMC.

10.5 Tailings Storage Facilities
The tailings storage facility (TSF) is located approximately 500 meters southeast of the
CIP Plant and is constructed in two phases (Phase 1 and Phase 2). The designed dam
height of Phase 1 is 18 m (dam crest elevation of 383m), with a storage capacity of 8
million cubic meters (Mm3). It was commissioned in September 2022, and the stored
tailings volume has reached the design capacity.
Phase 2 of the TSF is divided into four stages, which are summarized as follows:
. Stage 1
— Designed dam height: 21 meters
— Storage capacity: 24.60 Mm3, and
— Status: Construction completed and put into operation in November 2024
. Stage 2
— Designed dam height: 26 meters
— Storage capacity: 45.10 Mm3, and
— Status: Design completed, construction contract signed, and geotextile
material purchase contracts finalized.
. Stage 3
— Designed dam height: 31 meters
— Storage capacity: 59.40 Mm3, and
— Status: Construction has not yet begun.
. Stage 4
— Designed dam height: 37 meters
— Total storage capacity: 80.00 Mm3, and
— Status: Construction has not yet begun.
As of June 2025, the total TSF has accumulated a tailings volume of 19.73 Mm3, with a
remaining designed capacity of 60.27 Mm3.

11.2 Assessment of Workforce
For the production, the working schedule is 12 hours/shift, 2 shifts/day and ~350
days/year. There are 2-shifts personnel on, with 2 shifts off. RGG states the bad weather
could impact operation minimum only on the heavy snow that truck would stop.
It is SRK’s opinion that the numbers of the employees and their compositions are
reasonable. There are also sufficient manpower available around the project area.

The objective of this review is to identify and/or verify the existing and potential

13.2 Environmental and Social Review Process, Scope and Standards
The process for the verification of the environmental compliance and conformance for
the Raygorodok Project comprised a review and inspection of the Raygorodok Project’s

. Kazkhstan national environmental regulatory requirements; and
. World Bank/International Finance Corporation (‘‘IFC’’) environmental standards

The methodology applied for this environmental review of the Raygorodok Project
consisted of a combination of documentation review, site visit and interviews with

13.3 Environmental Legal Framework
The Code on Subsoil and Subsoil Use (‘‘Subsoil Code’’) is the primary legislation
governingKazakhstan’sminingindustry.Inaddition,otherlawsandregulationsaddress
environment-related matters, including the Environmental Code, Land Code, and Water
Code. This chapter summarizes the relevant legal framework applicable to mining
projects in Kazakhstan.
Code on Subsoil and Subsoil Use
On December 27, 2017, Kazakhstan adopted the Code on Subsoil and Subsoil Use (No.
125-VI ZRK), which came into effect on June 29, 2018. The law simplified the
application process for obtaining subsoil use rights. Since its adoption, the law has
undergone multiple amendments, with the most recent revision dated May 21, 2024.
According to Article 6 of the latest version of the Subsoil Law, the use of subsoil
resources must adhere to the principle of ecological safety and include measures to
prevent pollution and minimize adverse environmental impacts.
Regardingtheuseofsubsoilresources,miningcontractsinKazakhstanincludeanumber
of mandatory provisions related to environmental and social responsibilities:
. Subsoil users are obligated to provide funding for the training of Kazakhstani
personnel during the production period;
. Subsoil users are required to mitigate the consequences arising from subsoil use
activities;
. Subsoil users must bear the costs of research and development incurred during
production within the territory of Kazakhstan;
. Subsoil users are obliged to contribute financially to the social and economic
development of the region, as well as to the development of its infrastructure.
IIIH-137

=== PAGE 2733 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Environmental Code
The Environmental Code (No. 400-VI ZRK, January 2021) is the primary legislative
document stipulating environmental protection requirements in Kazakhstan. The
Environmental Regulation and Control Committee under the Ministry of Ecology and
Natural Resources of Kazakhstan is the main enforcement authority responsible for
issuing environmental permits and overseeing environmental compliance.
The Environmental Code sets out general requirements applicable to mining projects.
Non-compliance with these requirements may result in significant fines and penalties,
andcanevenleadtothesuspensionorterminationofsubsoilusecontracts.Accordingto
the Environmental Code, an environmentalpermit is mandatory if the operational facility
falls under Category I or Category II, with solid mineral production classified as
CategoryI.TheCodealsooutlinestheprocedureforobtaininganenvironmentalpermit,
which serves as an official document confirming that individuals or legal entities are
authorized to discharge pollutants.
The Environmental Impact Assessment (‘‘EIA’’) is a prerequisite for obtaining an
environmental permit. Therefore, an EIA must be conducted and approved by the
relevant regulatory authorities. The approval of an EIA report applies not only to new
projects but also to modifications of already approved projects. Mining projects may
require multiple EIA reports to cover various aspects such as greenfield development,
expansion, technological upgrades, and capacity increases. Furthermore, public
consultation is a mandatory component of the EIA process.
Subsoil users are required to obtain an environmental emission permit, with the
exception of emissions from mobile sources of pollution. Kazakhstan’s emission
permitting system is based on the ‘‘polluter pays’’ principle, meaning that developers
must pay fees for emissions in accordance with the terms set out in their permits.
Emission sources must comply with the emission limits specified in the permit.
Additionally, the law defines maximum allowable concentrations for pollutants at the
boundaries of sanitary protection zones around hazardous facilities.
Land Code
TheLandCode(No.442,June2003)allowslandtobedesignatedforspecificpurposes.It
stipulates that all landowners and land users — whether public or private — must not
endanger public health or the environment, pollute the land, or degrade soil fertility.
Theyarealsorequiredtoprotecttopsoilandundertakelandreclamation.TheLandCode
permits the state to acquire land for ‘‘public needs’’, which may include mineral
exploration and extraction. It also sets out the legal procedures for changing the
designated use of land.
Water Code
The Water Code (No. 481, June 2003) sets out the general procedures for the protection
of water resources, including the obligation to pay for water use and to safeguard water
bodies from pollution and depletion. Similar to the Environmental Code, the Water Code
requires permits for water intake, industrial water use, and wastewater discharge,
collectively referred to as ‘‘special water use.’’

13.5 Site Ecological Assessment
Thetopographyandlandscapeofthe projectareamaybealtereddueto thedevelopment
of the open-pit, processing plant, tailings storage facility, waste rock dumps, access
roads, office buildings, dormitories, and other associated infrastructure. The
construction and operation of the project may also lead to impacts on or loss of flora
and fauna habitats. Without effective management and rehabilitation of disturbed areas,
surrounding land may be contaminated, land-use functionality may change, and issues
such as desertification and soil erosion may be exacerbated.
SRK has reviewed multiple Environmental Impact Assessment (‘‘EIA’’) reports provided
for the project. These reports provide brief descriptions of the baseline flora and fauna
conditions in the project area. The region is characterized as typical bunchgrass steppe,
with low-growing herbaceous vegetation covering the surface. Smallpatches of forest are
present throughout the area, and mixed forests can be found within 50 to 70 kilometers.
Dominant tree species include pine, birch, and poplar. Understory vegetation in the pine
forests includes holly, bilberry, and various fern species. Meadows are widely distributed
in low-lying areas between forests and shrubs. Due to topsoil stripping and continuous
vehicle traffic, areas such as open pits, ore heaps, heap leach pads, roads, and their
immediate surroundings have little to no vegetation. However, vegetation in the
surrounding areas of the mine site remains in good condition, showing no significant
degradation. No rare, endemic, or endangered plant species have been identified within
the explored mining area.
The baseline EIA studies indicate that wildlife resources in the area are scarce, consisting
mainly of small rodents and bird species. Due to disturbance from vehicle movement,
earthworks, and human activity, wildlife is virtually absent within the industrial areas.
AccordingtotheminingEIAreports(2021and2022)andthetailingsfacilityEIA(2023),
there are no rare or endangered species listed in the Red Book of the Republic of
Kazakhstan found within the project area. However, the processing plant EIA (2019) did
mention the presence of Red Book-listed species within the EIA study area. Given the
proximity between the processing plant and the mining site, and the fact that the
processing plant EIA is older, SRK believes that the likelihood of rare or endangered
species being present in the vicinity of the current project area is low.
The Kokshetau National Park is located approximately 30 kilometers northwest of the
pit, and the Burabay National Park is located 48 kilometers to the east and northeast.
Given the distance, the EIA concludes that mining operations are not expected to have
any impact on the biodiversity of these national parks.
IIIH-141

=== PAGE 2737 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
The EIAs conclude that the project will not result in additional physical impacts on
vegetation. While dust deposition may suppress vegetation growth in adjacent areas, the
disturbance is expected to be localized. The impact on terrestrial fauna outside the
mining area is considered indirect, minimal, and acceptable. No changes in species
diversity or population numbers of terrestrial fauna in neighboring areasare anticipated,
and no loss of biodiversity is expected.
Through the implementation of resource conservation and emission reduction measures,
the project can minimize its impact on the landscape, soil, and biodiversity. The EIA
recommends several measures, including minimizing land disturbance during mining,
rational siting of infrastructure to protect water bodies, stockpiling and reusing fertile
topsoil for rehabilitation of disturbed areas, preventing soil contamination in adjacent
areas, and using native plant species for ecological restoration.
13.6 Water Management
In Kazakhstan, water pollution control is governed by a comprehensive legal and
regulatory framework aimed at protecting the country’s water bodies from
contamination. The primary legislation is the Water Code, which sets permissible
limitsforpollutants inbothsurfaceandgroundwater,ensuringcompliancewithnational
water quality standards. The regulations establish strict wastewater discharge standards
forindustriesandlocalauthorities,specifyingthresholdsforvariouspollutantsincluding
heavy metals, organic substances, and nutrients. Industries are required to implement
effective wastewater treatment systems to reduce harmful substances before discharging
treated water into local water bodies.
Thesurfacewatersystemintheprojectareaisunderdeveloped,withnowell-formedriver
network near the mine site. It primarily consists of intermittent gullies and shallow
seasonal lakes that dry up in the summer. A small river, the Arshaly River, is located 6
km southwest of the deposit. It is mainly fed by snowmelt and partially by groundwater.
Some stretches of the river dry up in summer, freeze in November, and thaw in April,
with spring floods typically occurring in April or May, lasting about 10 to 15 days. To
the north, 4 km from the deposit, lies a shallow freshwater lake, Shybyndykol,
characterized by reed and floating aquatic vegetation. The lake experiences high water
levels in spring, lower levels in summer and autumn, and stable levels in winter.
The project’s domestic water supply currently comes from two water wells. Water from
the wellsisextractedand purified,then storedin fourundergroundstoragetanks located
near the camp, each with a capacity of 100 cubic meters. The purified groundwater is
used for domestic purposes in the camp and office facilities.In addition to the previously
mentioned well water, the CIP (‘‘Carbon-in-Pulp’’) plant’s water supply also comes from
pit dewatering and tailings return water, with the majority of the water sourced from the
tailings return and pit dewatering.
Under Kazakhstan’s Water Code, the use of surface and groundwater and the discharge
of water require Special Water Use Permits. Available documentation shows that all
relevant permits have either been updated or are undergoing regular renewal processes.
The permit for pit water discharge allows for 458,250 m3 per year. In August 2022, the
project obtained a permit to abstract 1,000,000 m3 per year from Lake Shybyndykol.
However, current production needs are met entirely by pit dewatering and groundwater
wells, so no water is being drawn from the lake. These water sources are sufficient to
support a 6 Mtpa processing capacity. SRK recommends that the project implement a
sustainable water management plan to minimize impacts on natural systems, avoid
aquiferdepletion,andreduceeffectsonotherwaterusers.Theprojectshouldalsoengage
withkeystakeholders(i.e.,governmentagenciesandpotentiallyaffectedcommunities)to
identify any potential conflicts arising from water demand, local water dependence,
and/or existing conservation requirements.
IIIH-142

=== PAGE 2738 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
The project’s main potential negative impacts on surface and groundwater stem from the
improper discharge of untreated industrial and domestic wastewater. Key wastewater
sources include pit dewatering, process water from ore treatment, leachate from waste
rock dumps, contaminated stormwater from industrial areas, and domestic sewage.
According to the EIA, the site has two wastewater collection ponds with a total capacity
of 70,000 m3 (10,000 m3 and 60,000 m3, respectively), both lined with geomembranes for
waterproofing. During the site visit, SRK learned that there are currently two ponds
collecting pit dewatering. As mentioned in the EIA, one pond with a capacity of 60,000
cubic meters is in use, while the other, originally 10,000 cubic meters, has been expanded
to40,000cubicmetersasabackup.Thecollectedpitwaterisreusedforvariouspurposes
such as operations in the open pit, heap leaching, firefighting, road spraying, blasting,
and irrigation. Five emergency ponds are installed around the heap leach pad to mitigate
environmental pollution risks in case of emergencies. Fracture water downstream of the
tailingsstorage facility is collected and directed to apond adjacent to the tailings storage
facility. In addition, there are five monitoring wells around the tailings storage facility to
monitor groundwater quality. The project currently has three domestic wastewater
treatment facilities. Treated wastewater from two of these facilities is discharged into the
60,000 m3 pit water collection pond and then reused in the processing plant, while the
treated water from the third facility is reused directly in the processing plant.
The project’s CIP process uses the INCO method (SO /air) to destroy cyanide in tailings
2
slurry. Sodium metabisulfite serves as the SO source, with copper sulfate as a catalyst,
2
and lime is added as needed. Within a defined pH range and under catalysis by copper
ions, SO and air act synergistically to oxidize cyanide. The concentration of neutralized
2
cyanide is expected to be reduced to 20 mg/L. Process water and wash water from the
plant are recycled back into the processing circuit.
Soil samples collected in the operating area in 2021 showed contamination by cobalt,
arsenic, and chromium. However, water quality tests of the two wastewater ponds
conducted in 2021 indicated that concentrations of arsenic, copper, and lead were within
permissible limits. The project conducts monthly monitoring of cyanide levels in
groundwater at boreholes located in areas potentially affected by contamination.
According to several industrial environmental control reports, cyanide concentrations in
groundwater have not exceeded the maximum allowable limits. SRK observed that in
two groundwater monitoring reports from March 2025, the cyanide concentrations were
also below the regulatory limits. In addition, the treated wastewater monitoring report
from March 2025 indicated that parameters such as ammonia nitrogen, sulfate, and
chloride were all within the specified limits.
SRK recommends that water quality monitoring be conducted for both surface and
groundwater resources in the project area, including upstream and downstream
locations, and for any onsite water discharges. SRK also recommends the project
establish an effective drainage system to reduce the risk of water contamination.
13.7 Waste Rock and Tailings Management
AccordingtotheminingEnvironmentalImpactAssessment(‘‘EIA’’),thestrippedtopsoil
and waste rock generated during the mining process are stored separately in dedicated
waste rock dumps (‘‘WRD’’), using a layered stacking method. During the site visit, SRK
observed that there are five main waste rock dumps in the mining area. Currently,
Dumps No. 4 and No. 5 are still in use, while the other three are no longer receiving
waste rock.
IIIH-143

=== PAGE 2739 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
Tailings from the processing plant are discharged as slurry into the tailings storage
facility (‘‘TSF’’) after cyanide is destroyed using the SO /air oxidation method (INCO
2
process). Currently, there are two tailings storage facilities on site, TSF1 and TSF2,
located adjacent to each other. The TSF2 is currently undergoing expansion, with a plan
to increase its capacity from 8 million cubic meters to 80 million cubic meters, to be
carriedoutinfourphases.Aspartoftheexpansion,geomembranelinerswillbeinstalled
for seepage control. In addition, two diversion channels are designed to prevent erosion
of the TSF embankments caused by rainwater and snowmelt runoff, and to capture and
redirect stormwater and meltwater from the highlands into the TSF. The project has not
yet conducted detailed geochemical analyses of the waste rock and tailings to assess the
risk of acid rock drainage (‘‘ARD’’). A comprehensive geochemical assessment would
enable the company to identify potential problems in advance and prevent long-term
environmental risks. SRK recommends that the design and operation of the TSF should
be aligned with industrybest practices and comply with the Global Industry Standard on
Tailings Management (‘‘GISTM’’) to ensure safe and responsible tailings storage and
long-term environmental protection.
13.8 Air and Noise Emissions
Kazakhstan has established a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework aimed at
managing air quality and controlling pollution. The primary legislation governing air
pollution is the Environmental Code. Permitted emission limits are determined based on
international best practices and the latest scientific research. The Ministry of Ecology
and Natural Resources, along with local environmental authorities, is responsible for
implementingandenforcing thesestandards.Theseregulatorybodiesmonitor airquality
through regular inspections, data collection, and assessment of compliance with
established emission limits. Failure to comply with air pollution standards may result
in significant penalties, including fines, suspension of operations, and, in cases of serious
violations, criminal charges.
The project’s dust emission sources mainly include drilling, blasting, loading and
dumping, waste dumping, ore stockpiling, crushing, screening, cyanidation processes,
and the movement of vehicles and mobile equipment. The dust control measures
proposed in the EIA report primarily include the use of wet dust suppression
technologies, water spraying, and dust collectors. According to monitoring reports
provided by the project owner, dust, SO , NO , NO, and CO levels at monitoring points
2 2
have been tracked, with no exceedances observed.
The main sources of noise emissions at the project originate from mining and processing
operations, including drilling, blasting, loading, transportation, crushers, ball mills,
pumps, and other processing equipment, as well as the operation of vehicles and mobile
equipment.TheEIAreportindicatesthatlow-noiseequipment,noiseisolationmeasures,
and appropriate blasting techniques will be adopted as noise prevention measures.
However, the monitoring data provided by the mine do not include noise and vibration
monitoring results. During the site visit, SRK did not observe any significant noise
emissions at the boundary of the project area.

13.9 Hazardous Materials Management
Hazardous substances are characterized by corrosiveness, reactivity, radioactivity,
explosiveness, toxicity, flammability, and potential biological infectivity, posing
potential risks to human and/or environmental health. These substances are primarily
generated during project construction, mining, and processing activities, and include
hydrocarbons (i.e., fuels, waste oil, and lubricants), mineral processing reagents,
chemical and fuel containers, used batteries, medical waste, and paints.
Kazakhstan’s Environmental Code stipulates that the disposal of all hazardous waste
must not compromise soil quality or result in contamination. This involves strict
guidelines for the handling, storage, and disposal of such materials, requiring facilities
managing hazardous waste to obtain special permits. Entities found in violation of these
regulations are subject to enforcement actions, including fines and mandatory
remediation to restore land integrity and protect public health.
According to the ESG gap analysis provided by third-party evaluator Hudson Sandler,
the project still has some gaps in publicly disclosing responsible hazardous waste
management policies and in identifying, managing, transporting, storing, and disposing
ofallhazardousmaterials.However,the projecthascommittedtoresponsiblehazardous
waste management and plans to ensure that 100% of hazardous waste generated will be
handled by qualified third-party operators by 2024.
During the site visit, SRK observed that all used grease drums from the project were
placed in a designated storage area equipped with a concrete hardstand and secondary
containment facilities, and these drums were transported and disposed of by an external
specialized agency. Next to the mining contractor’s maintenance area, there is also a
dedicated facility for storing used grease drums, which are regularly handled by an
external specialized agency.
The project has recently constructed a new explosives magazine, which is scheduled to be
commissioned in early November this year. In addition, during the site visit, SRK also
observed that the project’s cyanide storage facility was well maintained and securely
protected. The project’s diesel storage area is equipped with underground tanks designed
tocollectanypotentialspills,therebyreducingtheriskofcontaminationfromleaks.The
company informed SRK that the project’s current cyanide management complies with
local regulatory requirements in Kazakhstan. SRK recommends that procurement,
transport, handling/storage, use, decommissioning, operational safety, emergency
response, and training related to cyanide at the project could also refer to the practical
principles and standards set forth in the International Cyanide Management Code.
13.10 Occupational Health and Safety
A good safety management system should include on-site training, site-specific policies,
safe operating procedures, risk management, use of personal protective equipment
(PPE), emergency response plans, incident reporting, first aid on site, designated safety
personnel, and routine safety meetings.
Currently, RGG has established a Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) management
system consisting of six key components:
. HSE standards and safety management plans,
. Policies, procedures, and processes,
. Training and onboarding,
IIIH-145

=== PAGE 2741 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
. Monitoring,
. Control and review, and
. Supervision, reporting, and communication.
As outlined in the HSE management standards developed by RGG in March 2024, the
system includes standards for HSE management, safety management, health
management, and environmental management. In addition, the company has
established several procedures related to occupational health and safety, covering
traffic management, incident investigation, and work permitting processes.
RGG has also developed multiple emergency response plans, each tailored to specific
potential emergency situations at different operational sites. In SRK’s view, RGG’s
occupational health and safety (OHS) system is generally comprehensive. The
above-mentioned standards, procedures, and plans provide the foundation of an
effective OHS management system.
Duringthesitevisit,SRKobservedthatsafetysignswereplacedinappropriatelocations
around the production area. Safety procedures and instructions were posted within work
zones, and moving mechanical parts were properly guarded and shielded. Guardrails had
been installed on all platforms. In addition, RGG provided workers with appropriate
personal protective equipment (PPE), such as safety helmets, reflective vests,
noise-reducing earplugs, and dust masks.
According to the documents provided, RGG conducts monthly statistical analyses of
safety-related incidents, including the type, cause, and time of occurrence. The
company’s Total Recordable Injury Frequency Rate (‘‘TRIFR’’) was reported as 0.98
in2022 and2.98in 2023.In comparison,theaverageTRIFRof InternationalCouncilon
Mining and Metals (ICMM) member companies was 2.66 in 2022 and 2.59 in 2023. After
interview with the operator, it was revealed that the increase in TRIFR in 2023 was
largely due to the construction of the CIP plant and the onboarding of a new plant
operations team. After targeted training and mitigation measures, the TRIFR has
significantly decreased in 2024 and the first half of 2025.
SRK recommends that the company continue maintaining detailed occupational safety
records and prepare incident analysis reports for any future safety incidents. These
reports should follow internationally recognized OHS practices, analyzing the causes of
injuries or near-misses and clearly outlining preventive measures to avoid recurrence.
13.11 Site Closure Planning and Rehabilitation
SRK has reviewed the Mining Plan for the Raygorodok North and South Mining Areas
— Volume VI Mine Closure and Rehabilitation Plan, as well as the Explanatory Note to
the TSF Expansion to 80 Million m3 — Mine Closure and Rehabilitation Plan, covering
the rehabilitation of open-pit mining operations, waste dumps, ore stockpiles, tailings
storage facility, and roads, and providing closure cost estimates. The estimated closure
and rehabilitation cost for mining operations is 2,269,373,170 KZT, and the estimated
cost for the TSF under the agricultural reclamation option is 694,759,558.5 KZT. The
closure plan also includes a brief post-closure monitoring plan, mainly covering
groundwater, surface water, wastewater, soil, and slope stability of the TSF.
IIIH-146

=== PAGE 2742 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
SRK considers that the above closure and rehabilitation plans do not cover all
operational facilities, and the study depth is limited. SRK was informed that the project
has not yet developed a detailed and comprehensive closure plan. It is recommended that
mine closure and rehabilitation be managed in accordance with internationally
recognized industry practices, and that a closure and rehabilitation plan be developed
to document the entire process. The mine closure planning process generally includes
identifying closure stakeholders (e.g., government, employees, communities), reaching
agreement with stakeholders on closure criteria and post-closure land use, establishing
reclamation objectives based on the intended post-closure land use, defining closure
responsibilities (based on agreed closure standards), developing a closure management
framework, estimating closure costs, and formulating a post-closure monitoring plan.
According to the provisions of Contract No. 486 dated June 19, 2000 for Gold
Exploration and Subsequent Mining in Burabay District, Akmola Region, the mine closure
rehabilitation fund is calculated at 0.3% of exploration and production costs. The
company stated that, based on actual costs incurred from 2014 to 2024, the total fund
payable amounts to 1,028,482,110.95 KZT. According to the statistics provided by the
owner, as of September 30, 2024, the balance of the mine closure fund account was
678,161,568.74 KZT, resulting in a funding shortfall of 350,320,542.21 KZT. While this
shortfall is not expected to have a material impact on the project, the Subsoil Code
stipulatesthatifactualmineclosureandrehabilitationcostsexceedthesecuredfund,the
subsoil user is obligated to provide additional financing for closure activities. In
addition, the mine operator has deported the ERP data of closure deposits under Mining
Contract 486, TSF Subsoil License, and Exploration Licenses 663–668 with a total
amount of USD3,144,054 as of June 30, 2025 (with an exchange rate of approximately
520 KZT/USD). The Client also provided bank transfer receipts (in Russian) of the
closure deposits for SRK’s review.
13.12 Social Aspects
This project is located in the Burabay District of Akmola Region, Kazakhstan, within
the administrative jurisdiction of the Uspeno-Yurievsky rural area. Akmola Region is
known for its unique natural and climatic conditions, picturesque landscapes, numerous
lakes, and resorts. The region also encompasses the Burabay National Park, Kokshetau
National Park, and the Korgalzhyn Nature Reserve. Burabay is an administrative
district of Akmola Region, with Shuchinsk as its administrative center. As of early 2022,
the population of Burabay District was 73,757, with main economic activities including
agriculture, tourism, and rail transport. The closest village to the project site is
Raygorodok, located approximately 2 km from the northern open pit area. Another
village, Nikolaevka, lies about 4 km west of the southern open pit area. However, SRK
did not observe further information on these two villages during this review.
According to the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) report, the project is not
located within the boundaries of any nature reserves or national parks. Furthermore,
there are no sites within the project area that are registered with the cultural heritage
authority as being of architectural value or of academic significance for the study of
Kazakhstani vernacular architecture. As part of the environmental and social
management system, SRK recommends the development of a Chance Finds Procedure
to be implemented in the event of the discovery of cultural heritage. No further
disturbance should occur until an assessment is conducted by qualified experts and
appropriate actions are determined. Additionally, any archaeological discoveries made
duringprojectactivitiesmustbereportedto therelevantKazakhstaniheritageauthority.

However,theEIAreportlacksenvironmentalandsocialbaselineinformationconcerning

more likely to experience adverse impacts from project development. The project should
identify all potentially affected Indigenous communities within the area of influence and
assess the nature and extent of direct and indirect impacts on their economic, social,

the rights, dignity, aspirations, culture, and natural resource-based livelihoods of
Indigenous Peoples should be fully respected.

between 2023 and 2025 due to project changes.

performance. This mechanism should prioritize the needs of the affected communities. It
should be culturally appropriate, accessible to complainants, easy to understand,
transparent, and capable of timely resolution. The existence and procedures of the
grievance mechanism should be clearly communicated to affected communities as part of

will be returned at the end of the LOM. Total recultivation (including mine closure and
rehabilitation) costs are estimated at USD19 million and are in compliance with
Kazakhstan regulations.

15 ECONOMIC ANALYSIS
The economic analysis presented in this section is based purely on the results of the
technical review provided above and some key assumptions and is provided for Ore
Reserveestimationpurposesonly.TheeconomicanalysisoftheCompanywasconducted
using conventional DCF techniques. The NPV was determined from the project’s cash
flow using a discount rate range of 5% to 15%. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was
performed to assess the impact of variations in capital cost, operating cost, and pricing.
15.1 Principal Assumptions
The cash flow estimate encompasses only the revenue, costs, taxes, and other factors
directly associated with the Company. The assumptions are as follows:
. The ROM and final product are based on the LOM schedule.
. Annual gross revenue is determined by applying forecasted metal prices and
payability factors to the annual recovered metals for each operating year. The gold
payability factor is assumed to be 99.2%.
. SRK does not account for future inflation or currency and cost fluctuations; costs
are assumed to remain constant over the LOM.
. The analysis assumes 100% equity financing, with no debt or associated financing
costs factored in.
. No salvage value is included in the economic analysis.
. Royalties, payable VAT, and income tax are accounted for in the technical
economic analysis.
. Working capital is assumed to be 30% of the first production year’s Opex in the
analysis.
. The reference or effective date for the analysis is 30 June 2025.

15.1.3Tax and Royalties
Royalties
Metal Extraction Tax (‘‘MET’’): A rate of 7.5% of the gold price is applied to the
containedmetalinallrockminedabovethesitecut-offgradeandisincurredatthepoint
of mining.
Emissions Tax: An emissions tax of USD0.05 per tonne applies to all processed ore.
Income Tax
An income tax rate of 20% is applied in accordance with Kazakhstan tax regulations.
Payable VAT
Payable VAT is assumed as follows:
. Output VAT is calculated at 12% of revenue for 2025, increasing to 16% effective 1
January 2026.
. Input VAT is assumed to be 20% of the output VAT amount.
15.1.4Depreciation
Capex is depreciated on a unit-of-production basis over the LOM using the straight-line
method, with no salvage value assumed.
15.1.5Working Capital
Working capital refers to the funds required to support operations prior to receiving
revenue from finished products. It is estimated at 30% of operating costs for 2026 and
will be returned at the end of the LOM. Over the course of the project, net working
capital is expected to be zero.

In the risk assessment, various risk issues have been assessed for Likelihood,
Consequence, and Overall Rating. SRK has used a matrix as described below.
The Likelihood of a risk is considered within a certain time frame, e.g., five years, as:
. Likely: will probably occur;
. Possible: may occur; or
. Unlikely: unlikely to occur.

=== PAGE 2755 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
The Consequence of a risk is classified as:
. Major: the factor poses an immediate danger to the Raygorodok Project that, if
uncorrected, will have a material effect on the Buritica Project cash flow and
performance and could lead to a project failure
. Moderate: the factor, if uncorrected, will have a significant effect on the
Raygorodok Project cash flow and performance; or
. Minor: the factor, if uncorrected, will have little or no effect on the Raygorodok
Project cash flow and performance
The overall risk assessment combines the Likelihood and Consequence of a risk and be
classified as Low (unlikely and possible minor risks, and unlikely moderate risk),
Medium (likely minor, possible moderate, and unlikely major risks) and High (likely
moderate and major risks, and possible major risks).
17 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
17.1 Geology and Resource
RGG Mine is an epithermal vein-type gold-silver deposit but it shares many
characteristics with porphyry copper deposits.
The drilling, sampling,sample preparation, analyses, security, and data verification meet
common industry standards and are appropriate for Mineral Resource estimation.
The RGG are continue a range of activities which embrace development of new targets
through surface drilling, and infill drilling for resource upgrades.
Apart from continuing to do infill drilling in existing mining, Exploration has been
focussed on the Contract Area and 6 Exploration Licenses, which are Mokhovoye,
Kovalyovka, Cordon, Regional Exploration (Areas 1 thru 6), Novodneprovka and
Sharyk.
17.2 Mining and Ore Reserve
RGG is planned as an open-pit operation. SRK conducted pit optimization to review the
current LOMP design, verified its reasonableness, and updated the LOM plan to guide
the extraction of eligible Mineral Resources. The open-pit mining method employed at
bothNRGandSRGfollowstheconventionalapproachofdrillingandblasting,followed
by loading and hauling. After reviewing the methodology, equipment list, and mining
services, SRK considers the mine to be operating in line with industry’s best practices.
RGG will primarily rely on contractors for both stripping and mining activities. The
mine will provide management, technical services, and supervisory staff to oversee
operations. The primary production mobile equipment, along with some ancillary
equipment, will be supplied by the mining contractor.
Overall, the mining methods applied at RGG are considered sufficient and reasonable to
support ongoing and future operations. Below are the recommendations:
. Preliminaryreviewindicatesthatnearbyinfrastructuredoesnotposealimitationto
the expansion of NRG. However, it is recommended to carry out further geological
investigations in the northern part of the pit to better define the lithology, as this
will affect the design of the ultimate pit boundary.
. ForSRG,preliminaryassessmentsuggeststhatnearbyinfrastructureisasignificant
constraint to expansion of the pit boundary. It is recommended that additional
trade-off studies are conducted before proceeding with any new pit design.
IIIH-160

=== PAGE 2756 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
17.3 Mineral Processing and Metallurgy
The metallurgical testwork conducted by SGS is relatively in-depth and comprehensive,
and the test results can serve as a reference for production optimization.
The CIP Plant adopts a conventional ‘‘gravity separation — CIP’’ process, producing
gold dore´ as the final product. From 2023 to June 2025, RoM throughput has ranged
between 4.7 Mta and 6.4 Mta with recovery rates ranging between 86% and 89%,
averaging of 87.3%.
The operational records indicate that the technological process is suitable for the ore
types of this project, and equipment configuration is considered reasonable, achieving
favourable technical performance.
SRK recommends collecting representative ore samples based on the LOM plan and
conducting test work with varying blend ratios of SRG to NRG ore to verify production
resultsandoptimizeprocessparameters.Additionally,representativetailingssamplesare
suggested be collected to explore recovery tests aimed at extracting more gold from the
tailings, thereby improving gold recovery rates.
17.4 Infrastructure
RGG project isan operating gold mine, the currentinfrastructure issufficientto support
present-stage operations.
17.5 Environmental and Social Issues
EIA reports have been prepared for the project’s main mining operation facilities,
including the mine, processing plant, and tailings storage facility. According to the
summary list of environmental permits and approvals provided, the tailings storage
facility expansion and the processing plant capacity expansion project (6 million tonnes
per year) have obtained the relevant environmental permits. No rare, endemic, or
endangered plant species have been identified within the mining area, and wildlife
resources in the region are scarce; wild animals are almost absent within the industrial
facility areas.
Currently, the project’sproduction water mainly comes from pit dewatering,waterwells,
and tailings return water, with tailings return water and pit dewatering accounting for
the majority of water used by the CIP plant. The water supply within the mining area is
sufficient to meet the processing capacity demand of 6 million tonnes per year. The
project uses the INCO process to remove cyanide from the tailings slurry. Process water
and wash water from the processing plant are collected and recycled back into ore
processing. However, the project has not conducted detailed geochemical assessments of
waste rock and tailings to evaluate the risk of acid rock drainage (‘‘ARD’’). A
comprehensive geochemical evaluation would help the company anticipate and address
potential issues, thereby avoiding long-term environmental risks. The current mine
closure and rehabilitation plan does not cover all operational facilities and lacks
sufficient depth of study.
Although the project has obtained the main permits required for current operations,
attention should be paid to the validity periods of environmental permits, and timely
renewal and acquisition of permits for newly built or expanded facilities should be
carried out in accordance with relevant laws and regulations of Kazakhstan. The project
should conduct detailed geochemical assessment of waste rock and tailings to assess the
risk of acid rock drainage. SRK recommends developing a comprehensive and detailed
mine closure plan, with regular updates, to avoid the risk of underestimating the mine
closure and rehabilitation costs. The recommendation for a comprehensive stakeholder
engagement plan and grievance mechanism will help the project strengthen its
community relations.
IIIH-161

=== PAGE 2757 ===
APPENDIX IIIH COMPETENT PERSON’S REPORT
17.6 Mine Economy
The economic analysis presented is based purely on the results of the technical review
provided above and some key assumptions and is provided for technical evaluation and
Ore Reserve estimation purposes only. The economic analysis was conducted using
conventional DCF techniques. The NPV was determined from the project’s cash flow
using a discount rate range of 5% to 15%. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was
performed to assess the impact of variations in capital cost, operating cost, and pricing.
SRK also conducted a single-factor sensitivity analysis for the project. The analysis
focused on metal prices, Capex, and Opex, each tested within a ±30% range. The results
showed that the project is most sensitive to changes in metal prices.

APPENDIX IV SUMMARY OF ARTICLES OF ASSOCIATION
This Appendix contains a summary of the articles of association of our Company
(the ‘‘Articles’’). As the information set out below is in summary form, it does not
contain all of the information that may be important to potential investors. As stated in
‘‘Appendix V — Documents delivered to the Registrar of Companies and Available on
Display’’ in this Prospectus, a copy of the Articles is available for inspection.
The Articles were adopted by our Shareholders on September 17, 2025 and will
become effective on the Listing Date. The following is a summary of certain provisions
of the Articles. The powers conferred or permitted by the Articles are subject to the
provisions of the Companies Ordinance, the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous
Provisions) Ordinance and other ordinances, subsidiary legislation and the Listing
Rules.
ALTERATION OF CAPITAL
Our Company may from time to time by ordinary resolution alter its share capital in
any one or more of the ways set out in section 170 of the Companies Ordinance, including
but not limited to:
(a) increasing its share capital by allotting and issuing new shares in accordance
with the Companies Ordinance;
(b) increasing its share capital without allotting and issuing new shares, if the funds
or other assets for the increase are provided by the members of our Company;
(c) capitalizing its profits, with or without allotting and issuing new shares;
(d) allotting and issuing bonus shares with or without increasing its share capital;
(e) converting all or any of its share into a larger or smaller number of shares; or
(f) cancelling shares:
(i) that, at the date of the passing of the resolution for cancelation, have not
been taken or agreed to be taken by any person; or
(ii) that have been forfeited.
Subject to the provisions of the Companies Ordinance and the Articles, our
Company may by special resolution reduce our share capital in any way.

PURCHASE OF OWN SHARES AND WARRANTS
Our Company may exercise any powers conferred or permitted by the Companies
Ordinance or any other ordinance from time to time to purchase our own Shares of any
class in the capital of our Company (including any redeemable shares) or to give directly
or indirectly by means of a loan, guarantee, the provision of security or otherwise,
financial assistance for the purpose of or in connection with a purchase made or to be
made by any person of any share in our Company. Should our Company purchase our

to be acquired rateablyor in anyother particular manner as between the holders of Shares
of the same class or as between them and the holders of Shares of any other class or in
accordance with the rights as to dividends or capital conferred by any class of Shares
provided that any such purchase or other acquisition or financial assistance shall only be
made or given in accordance with any relevant rules or regulations issued by the Stock
Exchange or the SFC from time to time in force.
In the case of purchases of redeemable shares, purchases not made through the
market or by tender shall be limited to a maximum price and if purchases are by tender,
tenders shall be available to all shareholders holding redeemable shares of our Company
alike.
‘‘Shares’’ referred to above include shares, warrants and any other securities carrying
a right to subscribe for or purchase shares of our Company which are issued from time to
time by our Company.
VARIATION OF RIGHTS
Subject to the provisions of the Companies Ordinance, if at any time the capital of
our Company is divided into different classes of shares, the rights attached to any class
(unless otherwise provided by the terms of issue of the shares of that class) may be varied
or abrogated, either with the consent in writing of holders representing at least
seventy-five per cent. of the total voting rights of holders of shares in that class or with
the sanction of a special resolution passed at a separate general meeting of the holders of
the shares of that class, and may be so varied or abrogated either whilst our Company is a
going concern or during or in contemplation of a winding up.
To every such separate meeting the provisions of the Articles relating to general
meetings shall mutatis mutandis apply, except that:
(a) the necessary quorum at such meeting (other than an adjourned meeting) shall
be two persons present in person or by proxy holding at least one-third of the
total voting rights of holders of the shares in that class;
(b) at an adjourned meeting the necessary quorum shall be one person holding
shares of the class or his proxy;

every share of the class held by them respectively; and
(d) a poll may be demanded by any one holder of shares of the class whether

TRANSFER OF SHARES
Any shareholder may transfer all or any of his shares by an instrument of transfer in
the usual or common form or in a form prescribed by the Designated Stock Exchange or
in any other form approved by the Board and may be under hand or, if the transferor or
transferee is a clearing house or its nominee(s), by hand or by machine imprinted
signature or by such other manner of execution as the Board may approve from time to
time. The transferor shall be deemed to remain the holder of the share concerned until the
name of the transferee is entered in the register of members in respect of the shares. Shares
of different classes shall not be comprised in the same instrument of transfer.
The Board may, in its absolute discretion, refuse to register the transfer of a share
which is not fully paid or on which our Company has a lien. The Board may also refuse to
register a transfer of a share unless:
(a) the instrument of transfer is in respect of only one class of share and is properly
stamped;
(b) in the case of a transfer to joint holders, the number of joint holders to whom
the share is to be transferred does not exceed four;
(c) subject to the Companies Ordinance, the instrument of transfer is lodged with
our Company accompanied by the certificate for the shares to be transferred
and such other evidence (if any) as the Board may reasonably require to prove
the title of the intending transferor or his right to transfer the shares; and
(d) the instrumentoftransfer is accompanied bypaymentofsuch fee, notexceeding
the maximum amount prescribed by the Stock Exchange from time to time, as
the Board may from time to time require.
If the Board refuse to register a transfer of a share, it shall within two months after
the date on which the instrument of transfer was lodged with our Company send to the
transferor and transferee notice of the refusal. Upon request by the transferor or
transferee, the Board must, within twenty-eight days after receiving such request, (a) send
to the transferor or transferee (as the case may be) a statement of the reasons for the
refusal or (b) register the transfer.

member or the person entitled by transmission to the share; and

1. FURTHER INFORMATION ABOUT OUR GROUP
(a) Incorporation of Our Company
We were incorporated in Hong Kong under the Companies Ordinance as a
private company limited by shares on October 22, 2007 under the name of Jinfeng
(HK) International Mining Company Limited (金峰（香港）國際礦業有限公司). Our
registered office is at Room 7508, Level 75, International Commerce Centre, 1
Austin Road West, Kowloon, Hong Kong.
The name of our Company was changed to Zijin Gold International Company
Limited (紫金黃金國際有限公司) on March 19, 2025.
As we were incorporated in Hong Kong, our corporate structure and operations
are subject to the Companies Ordinance, the Companies (Winding Up and
Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance and the Articles of Association. A summary
of certain provisions of our Articles of Association is set out in Appendix IV to this
Prospectus.
(b) Changes in the Share Capital of Our Company
As at the date of incorporation of our Company, our Company had an initial
registered share capital of HK$1 divided into one Share, which was allotted and
issued as fully paid to Zijin Northwest. On January 25, 2013, our Company allotted
545,999,999 Shares to Zijin Northwest at HK$1 per Share, and our share capital
increased by HK$545,999,999. On March 14, 2025, our Company further allotted
1,171,000,000 Shares to Gold Mountains (H.K.) at approximately HK$6.660974 per
Share, and our share capital increased from HK$546,000,000 to HK$1,717,000,000.
On May 6, 2025, our Company further allotted 558,000,000 Shares to Gold
Mountains (H.K.) at approximately HK$28.516129 per Share, and our share capital
increased from HK$1,717,000,000 to HK$24,258,000,000.
Immediately following the completion of the Global Offering but without
taking into account any Shares which may be issued upon the exercise of the
Over-allotment Option, 2,623,990,700 Shares will be issued as fully paid or credited
as fully paid.
Save as disclosed above and as mentioned in ‘‘— 1. Further Information about
our Group — (c) Written Resolutions of our Shareholders passed on September 17,
2025’’ below, there has been no alteration in the share capital of our Company since
its incorporation.

(f) Repurchase by our Company of our own securities
This paragraph includes information required by the Stock Exchange to be

(i) Provisions of the Listing Rules
The Listing Rules permit companies with a primary listing on the Stock
ExchangetorepurchasetheirsecuritiesontheStockExchangesubjecttocertain
restrictions, the most important of which are summarized below:
(A) Shareholders’ approval
All proposed repurchases of securities by a company with its primary
listing on the Stock Exchange, whether directly or indirectly, must be
approved in advance by an ordinary resolution of shareholders, either by
way of general mandate or by specific approval of a specific transaction.
Pursuant to the written resolutions of our sole Shareholder passed on
September 17, 2025, our Directors were granted a general unconditional
mandate (the ‘‘Repurchase Mandate’’) to repurchase Shares as described
above in the paragraphs headed ‘‘— 1. Further Information about our
Group — (c) Written Resolutions of our Shareholders passed on
September 17, 2025’’ in this Appendix.
(B) Source of funds
Repurchases of shares must only be funded out of funds legally
permitted to be utilized in this connection in accordance with the Articles,
the Listing Rules and the applicable laws of Hong Kong. A company may
not repurchase its own securities on the Stock Exchange for a
consideration other than cash or for settlement otherwise than in
accordance with the trading rules of the Stock Exchange from time to time.
V-4

=== PAGE 2813 ===
APPENDIX V STATUTORY AND GENERAL INFORMATION
(C) Trading restrictions
The total number of shares which a listed company is authorized to
repurchase on the Stock Exchange is such number of shares which
represents up to a maximum of 10% of the number of issued shares as at
the date of the resolution approving the repurchase. A company may not
issue or announce an issue of shares for a period of 30 days immediately
following a repurchase (other than an issue of securities pursuant to an
exercise of warrants, share options or similar instruments requiring the
company to issue securities which were outstanding prior to such
repurchase) without the prior approval of the Stock Exchange.
In addition, a listed company is prohibited from repurchasing its
sharesontheStockExchangeifthepurchasepriceishigherby5%ormore
than the average closing market price for the five preceding trading days
on which its shares were traded on the Stock Exchange.
The Listing Rules also prohibit a listed company from repurchasing
its shares on the Stock Exchange if the repurchase would result in the
number of listed securities which are in the hands of the public falling
below the relevant prescribed minimum percentage as required by the
Stock Exchange.
A listed company is required to procure that the broker appointed by
it to effect a repurchase of shares disclose to the Stock Exchange such
information with respect to the repurchase made on behalf of the listed
company as the Stock Exchange may require.
(D) Shares to be purchased
The Listing Rules provide that the shares which are proposed to be
purchased by a company must be fully paid up.
(E) Status of repurchased securities
The listing of all repurchased shares (whether on the Stock Exchange
or otherwise) is automatically canceled and the relevant documents of title
for those shares must be canceled and destroyed as soon as reasonably
practicable.
V-5

=== PAGE 2814 ===
APPENDIX V STATUTORY AND GENERAL INFORMATION
(F) Suspension of repurchases
A listed company may not make any repurchase of shares on the
Stock Exchange at any time after inside information has come to its
knowledge until the information is made publicly available. In particular,
during the period of one month immediately preceding the earlier of (a) the
date of the board meeting (as such date is first notified to the Stock
Exchange in accordance with the Listing Rules) for the approval of a listed
company’s results for any year, half-year, quarterly or any other interim
period (whether or not required under the Listing Rules) and (b) the
deadline for a listed company to announce its results for any year or
half-year under the Listing Rules, or quarterly or any other interim period
(whether or not required under the Listing Rules) and ending on the date
of the results announcement, the listed company may not repurchase its
securities on the Stock Exchange other than in exceptional circumstances.
In addition, the Stock Exchange reserves the right to prohibit repurchases
of shares on the Stock Exchange if a company has breached the Listing
Rules.
(G) Reporting requirements
Repurchases of shares on the Stock Exchange or otherwise must be
reported to the Stock Exchange not later than 30 minutes before the earlier
of the commencement of the morning trading session or any pre-opening
session (Hong Kong time) on the following Business Day. In addition, the
company’s annual report is required to disclose details regarding
repurchases of shares made during the year, including the monthly
breakdown of the number of shares repurchased, purchase price per
share or the highest and lowest price paid for all such repurchases, where
relevant, and the aggregate price paid for such purchases. The directors’
report shall contain reference to the purchases made during the year and
the reasons for making such purchases.
(H) Core connected persons
A listed company is prohibited from knowingly repurchasing shares
ontheStockExchangefromacoreconnectedperson,andacoreconnected
person is prohibited from knowingly selling his shares to the company.
(ii) Exercise of the Repurchase Mandate
Exercise in full of the Repurchase Mandate, on the basis of 2,623,990,700
Shares in issue immediately following the completion of the Global Offering
(assuming the Over-allotment Option is not exercised), could accordingly result
in up to 262,399,070 Shares being repurchased by us during the period in which
the Repurchase Mandate remains in force.

APPENDIX V STATUTORY AND GENERAL INFORMATION
(iii) General information relevant to the Repurchase Mandate
(A) Our Directors believe that it is in the best interests of us and our
Shareholders for our Directors to have a general authority from the
Shareholders to enable our Company to repurchase Shares in the
market. Repurchases of shares will only be made when our Directors
believe that such repurchases will benefit us and our Shareholders.
Such repurchases may, depending on market conditions and funding
arrangements at the time, lead to an enhancement of our net asset
value per Share and/or our earnings per Share.
(B) There might be a material adverse impact on our working capital or
gearing position (as compared with the position disclosed in our most
recent published audited accounts) in the event that the Repurchase
Mandate is exercised in full. However, our Directors do not propose
to exercise the Repurchase Mandate to such extent as would, in the
circumstances, have a material adverse effect on our working capital
requirements or the gearing levels, which in the opinion of our
Directors are from time to time appropriate for us.
(C) None of our Directors or, to the best of their knowledge having made
all reasonable enquiries, any of their respective close associates has
any present intention to sell any Shares to us or our subsidiaries if the
Repurchase Mandate is exercised.
(D) Our Directors have undertaken to the Stock Exchange that, so far as
the same may be applicable, they will exercise the Repurchase
Mandate only in accordance with the Listing Rules and the applicable
laws of Hong Kong.
(E) If as a result of a repurchase of Shares, a Shareholder’s proportionate
interest in the voting rights of our Company increases, such increase
will be treated as an acquisition for the purposes of the Takeovers
Code. Accordingly, a Shareholder (or a group of Shareholders acting
in concert, as defined in the Takeovers Code) could obtain or
consolidate control of our Company and become obliged to make a
mandatory offer in accordance with Rule 26 of the Takeovers Code.
Save as aforesaid, our Directors are not aware of any consequences
that would arise under the Takeovers Code as a result of any
repurchases pursuant to the Repurchase Mandate.
(F) No core connected person of our Company has notified us that he has
a present intention to sell Shares to us, or has undertaken not to do
so, if the Repurchase Mandate is exercised.

(g) Taxation of holders of Shares
The sale, purchase and transfer of Shares registered with our Hong Kong
branch register of members will be subject to Hong Kong stamp duty. The current
rate charged on each of the purchaser and seller is 0.1% of the consideration of or, if
higher, of the fair value of the Shares being sold or transferred. Profits from dealings
in the Shares arising in or derived from Hong Kong may also be subject to Hong
Kong profits tax. The Revenue (Abolition of Estate Duty) Ordinance 2005 came into
effect on February 11, 2006 in Hong Kong. No Hong Kong estate duty is payable
and no estate duty clearance papers are needed for a grant of representation in
respect of holders of Shares whose death occurs on or after February 11, 2006.
Intending holders of the Shares are recommended to consult their professional
advisors if they are in any doubt as to the taxation implications of subscribing for,
purchasing, holding or disposing of or dealing in the Shares. It is emphasized that
none of our Company, our Directors or parties involved in the Global Offering
accepts responsibility for any tax effect on, or liabilities of, holders of Shares
resulting from their subscription for, purchase, holding or disposal of or dealing in
Shares or exercise of any rights attaching to them.
